# Non-Uniqueness of Weak Solutions to the Unforced Two-Dimensional Euler Equations with Vorticity in $L^{1}\cap L^{p}$ , I: A Compactness Criterion and the Linear Analysis

**Authors:** Matei P. Coiculescu ††thanks: Department of Mathematics, New York University, Email: m.coiculescu@nyu.edu

## Abstract

This paper and its companion Part II prove that the incompressible Euler equations in the plane, without external force, admit two distinct renormalized weak solutions with the same initial vorticity $f$ , where $f$ is radial and nonnegative and lies in $(L^{1}\cap L^{q})(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ for every $q<\infty$ but is not bounded. One solution is radially symmetric and stationary. The other is $3$ -fold rotationally symmetric, is equimeasurable with $f$ at every time, and departs from $f$ in finite time; the two solutions are distinct in $L^{\infty}_{t}(L^{1}\cap L^{q})_{x}$ on $[0,T]\times\mathbb{R}^{2}$ for every $q\in(4/3,\infty)$ and every sufficiently large $T$ . In this first part we prove two ingredients. One is a compactness criterion: for a radial datum, a sequence of $3$ -fold rotationally symmetric solutions with converging data, whose non-radial moment is bounded below at some bounded time, has a subsequence converging to a second distinct renormalized weak solution. The other is the linear analysis for the building blocks of our multiscale datum. We show that the linearization of the Euler equations around the basic building block plus a small point vortex has an unstable eigenvalue in a space of $3$ -fold rotationally symmetric perturbations. This latter argument depends on rigorous interval arithmetic that we discuss more fully in Part II.

## 1 Introduction

We consider the incompressible Euler equations in the plane, in vorticity form:

$$ \partial_{t}\omega+v\cdot\nabla\omega=0,\qquad v=K_{BS}\ast\omega,\qquad\omega(t=0)=\omega_{0}. $$

Here $K_{BS}(x)=x^{\perp}/(2\pi|x|^{2})$ , $x^{\perp}=(-x_{2},x_{1})$ , denotes the Biot-Savart kernel, so that $v$ is divergence free and $\partial_{1}v_{2}-\partial_{2}v_{1}=\omega$ . There is no external force, and we call $\omega_{0}$ the datum.

For a smooth decaying datum, Equation (1) has a unique global smooth solution (Wolibner [22], Hölder [13]; see Kato [14]; a self-contained proof for compactly supported data is in Appendix B of Part II [8]). Yudovich proved in [23], for bounded domains, that a weak solution with bounded vorticity is unique: its velocity is log-Lipschitz, which closes an energy estimate for the difference of two solutions. For the plane, with vorticity in $(L^{1}\cap L^{\infty})(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ and square-integrable velocity, a complete proof is given in Theorem 0.3 and Appendix B.2 of [1]. For a datum in $(L^{1}\cap L^{p})(\Omega)$ , $1<p<\infty$ , global weak solutions exist (Yudovich for a bounded domain $\Omega$ [23], see the introduction of [24]; DiPerna and Majda for $\Omega=\mathbb{R}^{2}$ [11]). When $p>4/3$ the product $v\,\omega$ is locally integrable and Equation (1) has a weak formulation (Lemma 2.2, Definition 2.5), but the velocity is only Sobolev regular and Yudovich’s uniqueness argument does not apply. Whether his theorem extends to vorticity in $L^{\infty}_{t}L^{p}_{x}$ , $p<\infty$ , is the question of Section 1.1.1 of [5]. This paper and Part II [8] prove that, without force in the plane, uniqueness fails among renormalized weak solutions with vorticity in $L^{\infty}_{t}(L^{1}\cap L^{q})_{x}$ , for every $q\in(4/3,\infty)$ at once and for an explicit radial datum. The velocity of our datum is not square integrable (see below), whereas the planar theorem of [1] assumes it is, and the question of [5] is posed on $\mathbb{T}^{2}$ .

Uniqueness is known in several classes of unbounded vorticity. Yudovich proved in Theorem 1 of [24], in a bounded domain $D$ , uniqueness among solutions whose vorticity lies in every $L^{p}(D)$ with $p<\infty$ , with $\|\omega(t)\|_{L^{p}(D)}$ bounded, for all large $p$ , by a constant multiple of a growth function of $p$ satisfying a divergence condition of Osgood type. Taniuchi introduced uniformly local versions of these spaces on $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ and constructed global solutions in them [18]; uniqueness there under the same kind of divergence condition is proved by Chen, Miao and Zheng [7] and stated as Theorem 1.4 of [9], both crediting Taniuchi, and Crippa and Stefani gave a Lagrangian proof of uniqueness in localized Yudovich spaces (Theorem 1.6 of [9]). Vishik proved uniqueness in Besov-type spaces containing the local space $\mathrm{bmo}$ , under an additional integrability condition [19]. Bernicot and Keraani [3], Bernicot and Hmidi [2], and Chen, Miao and Zheng [7] gave spaces of unbounded vorticity with global existence, uniqueness or propagation of the class; Elgindi, Murray and Said [12] gave a local-in-time existence and uniqueness class whose solutions can leave it in finite time. Our datum satisfies none of these uniqueness criteria: its $L^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ norms grow exponentially in $p$ , it is not in $\mathrm{BMO}$ , its dyadic blocks grow too fast for the spaces of [19], and it is not odd in the angle. We leave the verification of these facts to the interested reader. So Theorem 1.1 contradicts none of these results.

With a radial force, Vishik [20], [21] proved non-uniqueness with vorticity in an $L^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ space, breaking the radial symmetry. In the account of Albritton, Bruè, Colombo, De Lellis, Giri, Janisch and Kwon [1], for every $p\in(2,\infty)$ there are a datum in $(L^{1}\cap L^{p})(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ (possibly zero) with velocity in $L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ and a force in $L^{1}_{t}(L^{1}\cap L^{p})_{x}$ whose Biot-Savart velocity lies in $L^{1}_{t}L^{2}_{x}$ , with uncountably many solutions with vorticity in $L^{\infty}_{t}(L^{1}\cap L^{p})_{x}$ and velocity in $L^{\infty}_{t}L^{2}_{x}$ . The unstable manifold of a steady vortex gives non-uniqueness only at time $-\infty$ ; Vishik’s self-similar background moves time $-\infty$ to time $0$ , but it is not an exact solution and requires the force (Section 0.1 of [1]). Without force, convex integration gives non-uniqueness for vorticity in $L^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ and $L^{p}(\mathbb{T}^{2})$ : Mengual [15] showed, for $2<p<\infty$ , that a truncated power-law vortex, a steady solution with vorticity in $(L^{1}\cap L^{p})(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , is the datum of infinitely many bounded admissible weak solutions, with velocity in $C_{t}L^{2}_{x}$ . In that result only the initial vorticity lies in $L^{p}$ : at positive times the vorticity of these solutions is known only as a distribution inside a growing disk, so they are not known to lie in the class $L^{\infty}_{t}L^{p}_{x}$ of the question above. Both solutions of Theorem 1.1, in contrast, have vorticity in $L^{\infty}_{t}(L^{1}\cap L^{q})_{x}$ for every $q\in(4/3,\infty)$ , so Theorem 1.1 answers that question in the plane, in the class in which it is posed. Bruè, Colombo and Kumar (Theorem 1.2 of [5]) obtained, on $\mathbb{T}^{2}$ , for some $p>1$ and a dense set of initial velocities, infinitely many weak solutions with vorticity in $C([0,1];L^{p}(\mathbb{T}^{2}))$ , which do not conserve energy. Outside the $L^{p}$ scale, convex integration also gives unforced non-uniqueness: [4] ( $L^{1,\infty}$ vorticity, bounded energy) and [6] (Hardy spaces $H^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , $2/3<p<1$ ).

In an instability construction without force, the background must be an exact solution. Ours is radial, hence stationary: infinitely many rescaled copies of one unstable vortex ring on disjoint annuli accumulating at the origin, with amplitudes increasing toward it. Inner rings rotate faster, and the task is to carry an instability from an inner ring outward through every ring in a time independent of the depth, uniformly in the number of interacting rings.

For $T>0$ and $1\leq q\leq\infty$ we write $X_{q}(T)$ for the space $L^{\infty}_{t}(L^{1}\cap L^{q})_{x}$ of functions on $(0,T)\times\mathbb{R}^{2}$ . Renormalized weak solutions in $X_{q}(T)$ , $q>4/3$ (after DiPerna and Lions [10]), and equimeasurability are defined in Definitions 2.5 and 2.4. The ring $\Phi$ of Definition 4.1 is a closed formula in $\log|y|$ times a fixed smooth cutoff; it is radial, $\Phi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , $0\leq\Phi<1$ , $\Phi\not\equiv 0$ , and $\supp\Phi\subset\{a\leq|y|\leq 1\}$ for an explicit $a\in(0,1)$ (Lemma 4.2). For $A_{1}>0$ , $\mu\in(1,2]$ and $\bar{s}\in(0,a/16]$ we put

$$ \begin{gathered}f=\sum_{k\geq 1}A_{k}\,\Phi(\cdot/r_{k}),\qquad A_{k}=A_{1}\mu^{k-1},\\
r_{1}=1,\qquad r_{k+1}=s_{k}r_{k},\qquad s_{k}=\bar{s}(2\mu)^{-k}\qquad(k\geq 1).\end{gathered} $$

The main theorem of the two papers is the following.

#### Theorem 1.1.

Let $\Phi$ and $a$ be as in Definition 4.1. There are $\mu\in(1,\frac{17}{16}]$ and $\bar{s}\in(0,a/16]$ such that, for every $A_{1}>0$ , the function $f$ of Equation (2) has the following properties. It is radial and nonnegative, $f\in(L^{1}\cap L^{q})(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ for every $q\in[1,\infty)$ , and $f\notin L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ . There is $T_{\star}\in(0,\infty)$ such that, for every $T>T_{\star}$ and every $q\in(4/3,\infty)$ , Equation (1) with $\omega_{0}=f$ has two distinct renormalized weak solutions in $X_{q}(T)$ , in the sense of Definition 2.5:

- (i) the stationary solution $\omega(t)=f$ , $t\in[0,T]$ ;

- (ii) a solution $\omega_{\infty}$ such that $\omega_{\infty}\in C([0,\infty);L^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{2}))$ for every $p\in[1,\infty)$ and, for every $t\geq 0$ , $\omega_{\infty}(t)$ is equimeasurable with $f$ and $3$ -fold rotationally symmetric.

More precisely, there is $t_{0}\in[0,T_{\star})$ such that $\omega_{\infty}$ and $f$ are distinct elements of $X_{q}(T^{\prime})$ for every $T^{\prime}>t_{0}$ and every $q\in(4/3,\infty)$ .

We do not treat $q\leq 4/3$ . No symmetry is imposed on the class; the $3$ -fold rotational symmetry of $\omega_{\infty}$ comes from the construction, where it removes the angular modes $\ell\notin 3\mathbb{Z}$ , among them the modes $\ell=\pm 1$ that contain the translations of a ring, and leaves the modes $\ell\in 3\mathbb{Z}$ , whose spectra we control under Hypothesis 4.17.

Theorem 1.1 concerns one explicit family of data. It says nothing about the kinetic energy or the vanishing viscosity limit. The velocity of $f$ is not square integrable: by Lemma 3.6, since $\supp f$ lies in the closed unit disk, $|K_{BS}\ast f(x)|=(2\pi|x|)^{-1}\int f$ for almost every $x$ with $|x|\geq 1$ , and $\int f>0$ .

The proof of Theorem 1.1 is divided between this paper and Part II [8]. This paper proves a non-uniqueness criterion (Section 3) and the linear analysis of the ring (Section 4), and it uses no machine computation. Part II proves that (N1)–(N3) of Hypothesis 4.17 imply Theorem 1.1 (Proposition 1.2 there), by a nonlinear construction followed by the criterion of Section 3, and it proves (N1)–(N3) (Theorem 1.3 there): (N1) and (N2) with rigorous interval arithmetic and (N3) by hand, in its Appendix A. Its Appendix B gives the existence theory for the global smooth solutions that the proof uses.

Section 3 follows the compactness theory of DiPerna and Lions for sequences of renormalized solutions, in a self-contained form for vorticity in $L^{\infty}_{t}(L^{1}\cap L^{2})_{x}$ , and proves a compactness criterion for non-uniqueness (Theorem 3.8). The form of it that Part II uses is the following conditional non-uniqueness theorem (Corollary 3.9 and Remark 3.10).

#### Theorem 1.2 (Conditional non-uniqueness).

Let $f$ be radial with $f\in(L^{1}\cap L^{q})(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ for every $q\in[1,\infty)$ . Suppose that there are data $f^{(n)}\to f$ in $(L^{1}\cap L^{2})(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ and, for each $n$ , a $3$ -fold rotationally symmetric renormalized weak solution $\omega^{(n)}$ of Equation (1) on $[0,\infty)$ with datum $f^{(n)}$ and vorticity in $L^{\infty}_{t}(L^{1}\cap L^{2})_{x}$ , with the following property: for some integer $m\geq 1$ , some real $\chi\in C_{c}^{\infty}((0,\infty))$ , some $c_{0}>0$ and $\bar{T}\in(0,\infty)$ , and some times $T^{(n)}\in[0,\bar{T}]$ ,

$$ \Big|\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\omega^{(n)}(T^{(n)},x)\,\chi(|x|)\,(\bar{x})^{m}\differential x\Big|\geq c_{0}\qquad\text{for all large }n, $$

with $x$ written as a complex number. Then Equation (1) with $\omega_{0}=f$ has, besides the stationary solution $\omega(t)=f$ , a renormalized weak solution $\omega_{\infty}$ with vorticity in $L^{\infty}_{t}(L^{1}\cap L^{2})_{x}$ that is $3$ -fold rotationally symmetric and equimeasurable with $f$ at every time and lies in $C([0,\infty);L^{q}(\mathbb{R}^{2}))$ for every $q\in[1,\infty)$ . For some $t_{0}\in[0,\bar{T})$ , $\omega_{\infty}$ and $f$ are distinct elements of $X_{q}(T^{\prime})$ for every $T^{\prime}>t_{0}$ and every $q\in(4/3,\infty)$ .

Since the moment in Theorem 1.2 vanishes for the radial function $f$ , its hypothesis says that the approximate solutions leave $f$ by a fixed amount, in one non-radial moment, within a time bounded independently of $n$ . The second solution is a limit of a subsequence of the $\omega^{(n)}$ .

For the datum $f$ of Theorem 1.1, Part II takes for $f^{(n)}$ the partial sum of the first $n$ rings of $f$ , with the innermost ring replaced by a seeded ring: a $3$ -fold rotationally symmetric copy of $\Phi$ , equimeasurable with it and close to it, that carries a small component along the unstable eigenfunction of Theorem 1.3 below. Figure 1 shows, for $n=10$ , the partial sum $f_{10}=\sum_{k=1}^{10}A_{k}\Phi(\cdot/r_{k})$ of the actual datum $f$ from which non-uniqueness occurs; $f^{(10)}$ differs from it only by the seed, which is invisible at this scale.

Left: $f_{10}$ against $\log_{10}|y|$ ; the rings sit at the scales $r_{1}=1>r_{2}>\dots>r_{10}\approx 10^{-32}$ , and their amplitudes $A_{k}=\mu^{k-1}$ grow toward the origin. Right: the same ten rings in a logarithmic polar picture, in which the distance from the center is an affine function of $\log|y|$ , so that all of them are visible; each ring is drawn without its amplitude, darker where $\Phi(\cdot/r_{k})$ is larger. The proof of Theorem 1.1 uses three explicit statements, collected in Section 4 as Hypothesis 4.17: (N1) and (N2) locate the zeros in the mode $\ell=3$ of the Evans function of the ring, an explicit holomorphic function, for every $G\in[0,\frac{1}{50}]$ , where $2\pi G$ is the circulation of a point vortex at the origin in the reference units of Definition 4.1; (N3) is an inequality between explicit numbers controlling the modes $\ell=\pm 6$ and $|\ell|\geq 9$ . Apart from the thresholds stated in (N1)–(N3), the only explicit numbers that the computer-assisted proof of these statements uses are the constants of the ring in Definition 4.1, which fix the building block of the multiscale datum; all other constants of this paper are used only through their existence. Without this hypothesis, Section 4 decomposes the linearization into angular modes (Lemma 4.5), reduces each mode to a linear second-order equation in $\xi=\log r$ , and defines the Evans function of each mode $\ell\geq 1$ (Definition 4.4). The Evans function is, up to sign, the Wronskian of the solutions of this equation that decay at the two ends (Lemma 4.6), and its zeros in $\{\real\lambda>0\}$ are exactly the eigenvalues there (Lemma 4.7). A simple zero of the Evans function gives an algebraically simple eigenvalue with an explicit Riesz projection of rank one (Theorem 4.8). Section 4 also bounds the real part of every unstable eigenvalue of the mode $\ell$ , for a radial vorticity that increases and then decreases in $r$ , by half the square root of an explicit double integral of the radial derivative of the vorticity over the region where it increases and the region where it decreases, which is nonincreasing in $\ell$ (Lemma 4.10). For the ring this integral is computed in closed form (Lemma 4.11), and (N3) makes the bound smaller than $\frac{9}{200}$ for $\ell=\pm 6$ and $|\ell|\geq 9$ . The section also proves a semigroup bound, uniform in $G$ , for all sufficiently large $|\ell|$ (Proposition 4.15), and constructs the semigroup of the linearization (Lemma 4.14).

The main result of the linear analysis is the linear instability of the ring, in the ring units of Definition 4.1, in the presence of a point vortex of small circulation $2\pi G$ at the origin, which stands for everything inside the ring. For an integer $s\geq 0$ let $X^{s}$ be the space of $3$ -fold rotationally symmetric $w\in H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2};\mathbb{C})$ supported in the annulus $\{\frac{a}{2}\leq|y|\leq 2\}$ .

#### Theorem 1.3 (Linear instability of the ring).

Assume (N1)–(N3) of Hypothesis 4.17, which Part II proves. For $G\geq 0$ let

$$ L(G)w=-\Big(K_{BS}\ast\Phi+\frac{G\,y^{\perp}}{|y|^{2}}\Big)\cdot\nabla w-(K_{BS}\ast w)\cdot\nabla\Phi $$

be the linearization of Equation (1) at the steady state $\Phi$ plus a point vortex of circulation $2\pi G$ at the origin. Let $\overline{G}\approx 0.006024$ be the constant of Definition 4.1. Then, for every $G\in[0,\overline{G}]$ and every integer $s\geq 0$ :

- (i) $L(G)$ , defined on $X^{s+1}$ , extends to the generator of a $C_{0}$ -semigroup $e^{tL(G)}$ on $X^{s}$ . Its spectrum in $\{\real\lambda>\frac{9}{200}\}$ is $\{\lambda_{*}(G),\overline{\lambda_{*}(G)}\}$ , with $\real\lambda_{*}(G)>\frac{211}{2500}$ . The eigenvalue $\lambda_{*}(G)$ has the eigenfunction $\phi_{*}(G)=g(|y|)e^{3i\theta}$ , with $g$ smooth and supported in $[a,1]$ and $\|\phi_{*}(G)\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}=1$ , and it is algebraically simple on the functions in $X^{s}$ of angular mode $3$ ; $\overline{\lambda_{*}(G)}$ has the eigenfunction $\overline{\phi_{*}(G)}$ , of angular mode $-3$ .

- (ii) $\lambda_{*}(G)$ depends continuously on $G$ .

- (iii) There is $C$ , depending only on $s$ , such that $\|e^{tL(G)}\|_{X^{s}\to X^{s}}\leq Ce^{\real\lambda_{*}(G)\,t}$ for $t\geq 0$ . For every $\sigma^{\prime}\in(\frac{9}{200},\min_{G^{\prime}}\real\lambda_{*}(G^{\prime}))$ there is $C^{\prime}$ , depending only on $s$ and $\sigma^{\prime}$ , such that $\|e^{tL(G)}(1-\Pi(G))\|_{X^{s}\to X^{s}}\leq C^{\prime}e^{\sigma^{\prime}t}$ for $t\geq 0$ , where $\Pi(G)$ is the spectral projection of $L(G)$ for $\{\lambda_{*}(G),\overline{\lambda_{*}(G)}\}$ , whose range is spanned by $\phi_{*}(G)$ and $\overline{\phi_{*}(G)}$ .

- (iv) The moment $\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\phi_{*}(G)(y)\,(\bar{y})^{3}\differential y$ , with $y$ written as a complex number, has modulus at least a constant $c>0$ independent of $G$ .

Theorem 1.3 collects Proposition 4.19, Lemma 4.7(2), Propositions 4.21 and 4.22, and Lemma 4.23. In Section 4 these are stated with the precise eigendata that Part II uses (Definition 4.20).

Part II uses these conclusions in a nonlinear construction, which we describe heuristically. Each ring of $f$ sees the rings inside it essentially as a point vortex of small circulation, so its linearization is the operator $L(G)$ of Theorem 1.3 for a small $G$ , and a perturbation along its unstable eigenfunction grows at a rate proportional to the amplitude of the ring: inner rings are faster. An approximation of $f$ that keeps finitely many rings carries a small multiple of the unstable eigenfunction on its innermost ring. This perturbation grows until the ring saturates; the non-radial moment of the saturated ring then kicks the next ring outward along its unstable eigenfunction, and that ring grows and saturates in turn. Ring $k$ needs a time of order $k/A_{k}$ to saturate, and $A_{k}$ grows geometrically toward the origin, so this relay reaches the outermost ring in a time bounded independently of the number of rings, and one bootstrap keeps every ring close to its expected evolution. This is why the datum is multiscale. A single unstable ring would not suffice: a perturbation of size $\varepsilon$ of a steady state needs a time of order $\log(1/\varepsilon)$ to reach a fixed size, which tends to infinity as $\varepsilon\to 0$ , so approximations that converge to the steady datum would not leave it in a bounded time; this is the reason why the unstable manifold of a steady vortex gives non-uniqueness only at time $-\infty$ . In our datum the approximation differs from $f$ only at the scale of its innermost ring, where the seed has a fixed size relative to the ring; it is small in $(L^{1}\cap L^{q})(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ only because that ring is small. So the instability starts at order one on the time scale of that ring, which tends to $0$ with the depth, and the relay carries it to the outermost ring in a bounded time. The instability is what produces a non-radial moment bounded away from zero. At saturation the perturbation of the outermost ring is, to leading order, a multiple of fixed size of its unstable eigenfunction and its conjugate, which lie in the angular modes $3$ and $-3$ . The moment $\int\omega\Psi$ with $\Psi(x)=\chi(|x|)(\bar{x})^{3}$ , where $\chi=1$ on the annulus of the ring, sees only the angular mode $3$ , like $p^{\mathrm{out}}_{3}$ (Definition 2.3), and on the unstable eigenfunction it is the moment of Theorem 1.3(iv), which is bounded away from zero uniformly in $G$ . So this moment of the outermost ring has modulus at least a constant $c_{0}>0$ independent of the number of rings, while it vanishes for the radial datum $f$ . This is the hypothesis of Theorem 1.2, which gives the second solution as a limit of the approximate solutions. Section 1.2 of Part II lists the definitions and results of this paper that it uses.

The main idea of a linear instability in physical coordinates driving the non-uniqueness mechanism, the use of non-monotone unstable radial vortices and of a multiscale datum, and the overall strategy of the proof are due to the author. Within this strategy, the detailed proofs and estimates, the code for the computer-assisted verification in Part II and the text were largely produced with Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), under the direction of the author. The author has checked all proofs by hand and takes full responsibility for the paper.
