## 2 Preliminaries

### 2.1 Conventions

We identify $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ with $\mathbb{C}$ , writing $x=(x_{1},x_{2})=x_{1}+ix_{2}$ when convenient, and $\bar{x}$ for the complex conjugate; $|x|$ is the Euclidean norm; for a matrix or an array of numbers, $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm of the array of its entries, and for a matrix $M$ we write $\|M\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ for its operator norm. For $r>0$ , $B_{r}=\{|x|<r\}$ and $\overline{B}_{r}$ is its closure; $|S|$ is the Lebesgue measure of a measurable set $S\subset\mathbb{R}^{2}$ . The overline thus denotes complex conjugation, of numbers and of functions, and the closure of a set; it is also part of the names of some fixed objects, such as the radial background $\overline{\omega}$ of Section 4 and the constants $\overline{G}$ , $\bar{s}$ and $\bar{T}$ . Which meaning is intended will always be clear from the context. We use polar coordinates $x=r(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$ , with $\textbf{e}_{r}=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$ and $\textbf{e}_{\theta}=(-\sin\theta,\cos\theta)$ . For $\theta\in\mathbb{R}$ , $\mathsf{O}_{\theta}$ is the rotation of $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ by the angle $\theta$ (multiplication by $e^{i\theta}$ ), and $\mathsf{O}=\mathsf{O}_{2\pi/3}$ . For an integer $m\geq 1$ , a function $g$ on $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ is $m$ -fold rotationally symmetric if and only if $g\circ\mathsf{O}_{2\pi/m}=g$ almost everywhere, and radial if and only if $g\circ\mathsf{O}_{\theta}=g$ almost everywhere for all $\theta$ . If $\theta\mapsto g(re^{i\theta})$ is integrable on $[0,2\pi]$ for almost every $r>0$ (by Fubini’s theorem in polar coordinates, this holds for every $g\in L^{1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ ) and $\ell\in\mathbb{Z}$ , the angular mode $\ell$ of $g$ is $g_{\ell}(r)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}g(re^{i\theta})e^{-i\ell\theta}\differential\theta$ , defined for almost every $r>0$ . If $g\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , then $g=\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb{Z}}g_{\ell}(r)e^{i\ell\theta}$ in $L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , and $g$ is $m$ -fold rotationally symmetric if and only if $g_{\ell}=0$ for all $\ell\notin m\mathbb{Z}$ .

The Biot-Savart kernel is $K_{BS}(x)=x^{\perp}/(2\pi|x|^{2})$ with $x^{\perp}=(-x_{2},x_{1})$ , and $\nabla^{\perp}=(-\partial_{2},\partial_{1})$ . For a vorticity $\omega$ we write $v=K_{BS}\ast\omega$ whenever the integral converges. If $\omega\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , then the stream function $\psi(x)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int\log|x-y|\,\omega(y)\differential y$ satisfies $v=\nabla^{\perp}\psi$ , $\Delta\psi=\omega$ and $\partial_{1}v_{2}-\partial_{2}v_{1}=\omega$ (Lemma 2.1(d) below). In polar coordinates these sign conventions read $v\cdot\textbf{e}_{r}=-r^{-1}\partial_{\theta}\psi$ and $v\cdot\textbf{e}_{\theta}=\partial_{r}\psi$ . For a vector field $u$ we write $\nabla u$ for the matrix $(\partial_{l}u_{i})_{i,l=1,2}$ , so that $\operatorname{tr}\nabla u=\divop u$ .

Functions are complex valued unless we say otherwise; vorticities and velocities are real. For a multi-index $\gamma=(\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2})\in\mathbb{N}_{0}^{2}$ we write $\partial^{\gamma}=\partial_{1}^{\gamma_{1}}\partial_{2}^{\gamma_{2}}$ , $|\gamma|=\gamma_{1}+\gamma_{2}$ , $\zeta^{2\gamma}=\zeta_{1}^{2\gamma_{1}}\zeta_{2}^{2\gamma_{2}}$ for $\zeta\in\mathbb{R}^{2}$ , $\beta\leq\gamma$ if $\beta_{1}\leq\gamma_{1}$ and $\beta_{2}\leq\gamma_{2}$ , and $\binom{\gamma}{\beta}=\binom{\gamma_{1}}{\beta_{1}}\binom{\gamma_{2}}{\beta_{2}}$ ; here $\mathbb{N}=\{1,2,\dots\}$ , $\mathbb{N}_{0}=\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}$ and $m\mathbb{N}=\{m,2m,\dots\}$ . For an integer $k\geq 0$ and an open set $V\subset\mathbb{R}^{2}$ , $H^{k}(V)$ is the Sobolev space with norm $\|g\|_{H^{k}(V)}^{2}=\sum_{|\gamma|\leq k}\|\partial^{\gamma}g\|_{L^{2}(V)}^{2}$ , and $H^{k}=H^{k}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ . Sobolev norms of vector and matrix fields are summed over the entries; for instance $\|\nabla u\|_{H^{k}}^{2}=\sum_{i,l}\|\partial_{l}u_{i}\|_{H^{k}}^{2}$ . For a vector or matrix field $F$ on $V$ and $1\leq q\leq\infty$ we put $\|F\|_{L^{q}(V)}=\|\,|F|\,\|_{L^{q}(V)}$ , where $|F|$ is the Euclidean norm of the array of entries; for $q=2$ this agrees with the sum over the entries. For a vector field $F$ on $V$ we put $\|F\|_{W^{1,\infty}(V)}=\operatorname{ess\,sup}_{V}|F|+\operatorname{ess\,sup}_{V}|\nabla F|$ .

For a function or vector field $h$ of class $C^{q}$ near a point $x$ , we write $\nabla^{q}h(x)$ for the array of all partial derivatives of order $q$ of the components of $h$ at $x$ , one entry for each ordered $q$ -tuple of directions, so that $|\nabla^{q}h(x)|$ is its Euclidean norm. For an integer $k\geq 0$ , a closed set $U\subset\mathbb{R}^{2}$ and $h$ of class $C^{k}$ on a neighborhood of $U$ , we put $\|h\|_{C^{k}(U)}=\sum_{q=0}^{k}\sup_{x\in U}|\nabla^{q}h(x)|$ ; in particular $|\partial^{\gamma}h(x)|\leq\|h\|_{C^{k}(U)}$ for $x\in U$ and $|\gamma|\leq k$ , and $C^{k}(U)$ denotes the space of such $h$ with finite norm. The Fourier transform is $\hat{g}(\zeta)=\int g(x)e^{-ix\cdot\zeta}\differential x$ , so that $\|\partial^{\gamma}g\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}^{2}=(2\pi)^{-2}\int\zeta^{2\gamma}|\hat{g}(\zeta)|^{2}\differential\zeta$ by Plancherel’s theorem.

We put $\langle t\rangle=(1+t^{2})^{1/2}$ for $t\in\mathbb{R}$ and $\log_{+}x=\max\{\log x,0\}$ for $x>0$ . For $x>0$ and an integer $p\geq 0$ we put

$$ I_{p}(x)=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-xu}(1+u)^{p}\differential u, $$

a finite (as $x>0$ ), decreasing function of $x$ .

Constants that enter a later choice of parameters carry their own names, and their dependence is stated where they are defined. The letter $C$ denotes a constant that enters no later choice; its dependence is stated each time, and within one proof its value may change from line to line. For a function $u$ and a nonnegative function $g$ , $u=O(g)$ as $r\to r_{0}$ means that $|u|\leq Cg$ in a neighborhood of $r_{0}$ for some constant $C$ .

Let $I$ be an interval and $X$ a Banach space. A function $F\colon I\to X$ is strongly measurable if it is an almost everywhere limit of simple functions $\sum_{i=1}^{k}\mathbf{1}_{E_{i}}(t)x_{i}$ , with $E_{i}\subset I$ measurable and $x_{i}\in X$ , and weakly measurable if $t\mapsto\Lambda(F(t))$ is measurable for every $\Lambda\in X^{*}$ . We use Pettis’s theorem [17]: if $X$ is separable, then $F$ is strongly measurable if and only if it is weakly measurable. The Bochner spaces $L^{\infty}(I;X)$ and $L^{1}(I;X)$ consist of the strongly measurable $F$ for which $t\mapsto\|F(t)\|_{X}$ is essentially bounded, respectively integrable, modulo equality almost everywhere.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{2}$ be a measurable set. For $b\in[1,\infty)$ , $L^{\infty}(I;L^{b}(\Omega))$ and $L^{1}(I;L^{b}(\Omega))$ are the Bochner spaces, whose elements we identify with measurable functions on $I\times\Omega$ ; a measurable $u$ on $I\times\Omega$ lies in them if and only if $t\mapsto\|u(t)\|_{L^{b}(\Omega)}$ is essentially bounded, respectively integrable, by Pettis’s theorem: $L^{b}(\Omega)$ is separable, and for $\phi\in L^{b^{\prime}}(\Omega)$ , $1/b+1/b^{\prime}=1$ , the function $t\mapsto\int u(t)\phi$ , defined for almost every $t$ , is measurable by Tonelli’s theorem applied to the positive and negative parts of the real and imaginary parts of $u\phi$ . We write $L^{\infty}(I;L^{\infty}(\Omega))$ for $L^{\infty}(I\times\Omega)$ , and $L^{1}(I;L^{\infty}(\Omega))$ for the set of measurable $u$ on $I\times\Omega$ with $\int_{I}\|u(t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\differential t<\infty$ . Intersections such as $L^{\infty}(I;(L^{1}\cap L^{\infty})(\Omega))$ are intersections of these spaces; a space with $W^{1,a}(\Omega)$ in place of $L^{b}(\Omega)$ consists of the $w$ for which $w$ and its distributional gradient in $x$ lie in the corresponding space with $L^{a}(\Omega)$ ; the subscript $\mathrm{loc}$ on the time interval means that the condition holds on $J\times\Omega$ for every compact interval $J\subset I$ , on $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ that it holds on $I\times B_{R}$ for every $R>0$ , and on both that it holds on $J\times B_{R}$ for all such $J$ and $R$ .

For $T>0$ and $1\leq q\leq\infty$ , the space $X_{q}(T)$ of Section 1, written $L^{\infty}_{t}(L^{1}\cap L^{q})_{x}$ there, is the Bochner space $L^{\infty}\big(0,T;(L^{1}\cap L^{q})(\mathbb{R}^{2})\big)$ just described, with $\|\omega\|_{(L^{1}\cap L^{q})(\mathbb{R}^{2})}=\|\omega\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}+\|\omega\|_{L^{q}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}$ ; and $\mathcal{D}_{T}=\{\varphi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{2}):\supp\varphi\subset(-\infty,T)\times\mathbb{R}^{2}\}$ . $\mathrm{Lip}_{0}$ is the set of Lipschitz functions $\Upsilon\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ with $\Upsilon(0)=0$ . For $g\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ we put $\Gamma_{g}(r)=\int_{B_{r}}g$ .

A $C_{0}$ -semigroup $(S(t))_{t\geq 0}$ on a Banach space $X$ is a family of bounded operators with $S(0)$ the identity, $S(t+s)=S(t)S(s)$ , and $t\mapsto S(t)x$ continuous for all $x\in X$ ; its generator $A$ is $Ax=\lim_{h\downarrow 0}h^{-1}(S(h)x-x)$ on the set $D(A)$ of $x$ for which the limit exists.

### 2.2 The Biot-Savart Law

We split $K_{BS}=K_{BS}^{\mathrm{nr}}+K_{BS}^{\mathrm{fr}}$ with $K_{BS}^{\mathrm{nr}}=\mathbf{1}_{B_{1}}K_{BS}$ . By Lemma 2.1(a) below, $\|K_{BS}^{\mathrm{nr}}\|_{L^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}^{s}=(2\pi)^{1-s}/(2-s)$ for $s\in[1,2)$ , and $|K_{BS}^{\mathrm{fr}}(z)|\leq\min\{1,|z|^{-1}\}/(2\pi)$ for $z\in\mathbb{R}^{2}$ .

#### Lemma 2.1.

The kernel $K_{BS}$ has the following properties.

- (a) For $z\neq 0$ , $i,l\in\{1,2\}$ and $\rho>0$ , $|K_{BS}(z)|=(2\pi|z|)^{-1}$ , $|\partial_{l}(K_{BS})_{i}(z)|\leq(2\pi|z|^{2})^{-1}$ and $\int_{B_{\rho}}|K_{BS}|\differential z=\rho$ .

- (b) Let $g\in(L^{1}\cap L^{\infty})(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ . Then for every $x\in\mathbb{R}^{2}$ ,

$$ \big(|K_{BS}|\ast|g|\big)(x)\leq\Big(\frac{2\|g\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\|g\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}}{\pi}\Big)^{1/2}. $$

In particular the integral defining $K_{BS}\ast g(x)$ converges absolutely for every $x$ , and $\|K_{BS}\ast g\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\leq\big(2\|g\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\|g\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}/\pi\big)^{1/2}$ .

- (c) Let $\rho,R>0$ and let $g\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ vanish outside $B_{\rho}$ . Then $K_{BS}\ast g$ is defined almost everywhere, and $\|K_{BS}\ast g\|_{L^{2}(B_{R})}\leq(R+\rho)\|g\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}$ .

- (d) Let $g\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ and $u=K_{BS}\ast g$ . Then $u\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , $\partial^{\gamma}u=K_{BS}\ast\partial^{\gamma}g$ for every $\gamma$ , $u=\nabla^{\perp}\psi$ with $\psi(x)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int\log|x-y|\,g(y)\differential y$ , $\Delta\psi=g$ , $\divop u=0$ and $\partial_{1}u_{2}-\partial_{2}u_{1}=g$ . Moreover $\sum_{i,l=1}^{2}\|\partial_{l}\partial^{\gamma}u_{i}\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}^{2}=\|\partial^{\gamma}g\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}^{2}$ for every $\gamma$ , and hence $\|\nabla u\|_{H^{k}}=\|g\|_{H^{k}}$ for every integer $k\geq 0$ .

- (e) Let $g\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ and $R>0$ . Then $\int_{B_{R}}\big(|K_{BS}|\ast|g|\big)\differential x\leq R\,\|g\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}$ . In particular the integral defining $K_{BS}\ast g$ converges absolutely almost everywhere, $K_{BS}\ast g\in L^{1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , and $\divop(K_{BS}\ast g)=0$ in $\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ .

#### Proof.

(a) The first identity holds because $|x^{\perp}|=|x|$ , and integration in polar coordinates gives $\int_{B_{\rho}}(2\pi|z|)^{-1}\differential z=\rho$ . Since $2\pi K_{BS}(z)=(-z_{2},z_{1})/|z|^{2}$ , the derivatives $2\pi\partial_{l}(K_{BS})_{i}$ are, up to sign, the numbers $\partial_{l}(z_{k}/|z|^{2})=\delta_{lk}|z|^{-2}-2z_{l}z_{k}|z|^{-4}$ , whose modulus is $|z_{k^{\prime}}^{2}-z_{k}^{2}|/|z|^{4}\leq|z|^{-2}$ if $l=k$ (where $k^{\prime}\neq k$ ) and $2|z_{1}z_{2}|/|z|^{4}\leq|z|^{-2}$ if $l\neq k$ .

(b) We may assume $g\neq 0$ . For arbitrary $r>0$ , (a) gives, after splitting the integral into the near field $\{|z|<r\}$ and the far field $\{|z|\geq r\}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle 2\pi\big(|K_{BS}|\ast|g|\big)(x) \displaystyle\leq\|g\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\int_{B_{r}}\frac{\differential z}{|z|}+\frac{1}{r}\int_{|z|\geq r}|g(x-z)|\differential z \displaystyle\leq 2\pi r\|g\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}+\frac{\|g\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}}{r}, $$

and choosing $r=(\|g\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}/(2\pi\|g\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}))^{1/2}$ gives

$$ 2\pi(|K_{BS}|\ast|g|)(x)\leq 2(2\pi\|g\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\|g\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})})^{1/2}, $$

which is the claim. The rest follows from $|K_{BS}\ast g|\leq|K_{BS}|\ast|g|$ .

(c) For $|x|<R$ and $|x-z|<\rho$ , we have $|z|<\rho+R$ , so, as $g$ vanishes outside $B_{\rho}$ , $K_{BS}\ast g(x)=\int_{B_{R+\rho}}K_{BS}(z)g(x-z)\differential z$ for $x\in B_{R}$ , and Minkowski’s integral inequality and (a) give $\big\|\int_{B_{R+\rho}}|K_{BS}(z)||g(\cdot-z)|\differential z\big\|_{L^{2}(B_{R})}\leq(R+\rho)\|g\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}$ . In particular the integral converges absolutely almost everywhere on $B_{R}$ , for every $R>0$ .

(d) Let $\supp g\subset B_{\rho}$ . Since $K_{BS}$ and $\log|\cdot|$ are locally integrable, differentiation under the integral sign shows that $u,\psi\in C^{\infty}$ , $\partial^{\gamma}u=K_{BS}\ast\partial^{\gamma}g$ and $\partial^{\gamma}\psi=\frac{1}{2\pi}\log|\cdot|\ast\partial^{\gamma}g$ . Writing $\partial_{j}g(x-z)=-\partial_{z_{j}}[g(x-z)]$ and integrating by parts on $\{|z|>\varepsilon\}$ , with a boundary term at most $\varepsilon|\log\varepsilon|\sup|g|\to 0$ , we get $\partial_{j}\psi(x)=\int\frac{z_{j}}{2\pi|z|^{2}}g(x-z)\differential z$ . Hence $u=\nabla^{\perp}\psi$ , so $\divop u=-\partial_{1}\partial_{2}\psi+\partial_{2}\partial_{1}\psi=0$ and $\Delta\psi=\partial_{1}u_{2}-\partial_{2}u_{1}$ . Fix $x$ , put $h(z)=g(x-z)$ , and use polar coordinates $z=re^{i\theta}$ , in which $z\cdot\nabla_{z}=r\partial_{r}$ . Since $\partial_{l}u=K_{BS}\ast\partial_{l}g$ and $(\partial_{l}g)(x-z)=-\partial_{z_{l}}h(z)$ ,

$$ (\partial_{1}u_{2}-\partial_{2}u_{1})(x)=-\int\frac{z\cdot\nabla_{z}h}{2\pi|z|^{2}}\differential z=-\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\!\!\int_{0}^{\infty}\partial_{r}h\differential r\differential\theta=g(x), $$

because $(K_{BS})_{2}\partial_{1}h-(K_{BS})_{1}\partial_{2}h=z\cdot\nabla_{z}h/(2\pi|z|^{2})$ and $\int_{0}^{\infty}\partial_{r}h\differential r=-h(0)=-g(x)$ ; the integrand is integrable, as $|\partial_{r}h|\leq|\nabla h|$ and $h$ has compact support. Hence $\Delta\psi=g$ .

For $|x|\geq 2\rho$ and $|y|<\rho$ we have $|x-y|\geq|x|/2$ ; differentiating under the integral sign, with $|\nabla\log|z||=|z|^{-1}$ and $|\partial_{i}\partial_{j}\log|z||=|\partial_{j}(z_{i}/|z|^{2})|\leq|z|^{-2}$ (proof of (a)), gives $|\nabla\psi(x)|\leq\|g\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}/(\pi|x|)$ and $|\partial_{i}\partial_{j}\psi(x)|\leq 2\|g\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}/(\pi|x|^{2})$ for $|x|\geq 2\rho$ . Two integrations by parts on $B_{r}$ give $\int_{B_{r}}\sum_{i,j}(\partial_{i}\partial_{j}\psi)^{2}\differential x=\int_{B_{r}}(\Delta\psi)^{2}\differential x+\mathcal{B}_{r}$ , where $\mathcal{B}_{r}$ is a sum of integrals over $\partial B_{r}$ of products of a first and a second derivative of $\psi$ ; for $r\geq 2\rho$ the bounds above give $|\mathcal{B}_{r}|\leq Cr\cdot r^{-1}r^{-2}\|g\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}^{2}$ with $C$ absolute. Letting $r\to\infty$ gives $\sum_{i,j}\|\partial_{i}\partial_{j}\psi\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}^{2}=\|g\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}^{2}$ . The entries of $\nabla u$ are, up to sign, the second derivatives of $\psi$ , so $\sum_{i,l}\|\partial_{l}u_{i}\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}^{2}=\|g\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}^{2}$ . Replacing $g$ by $\partial^{\gamma}g$ , whose velocity is $\partial^{\gamma}u$ , and summing over $|\gamma|\leq k$ gives the rest. For complex $g$ we apply all of this to the real and imaginary parts.

(e) Let $D$ be a disk of radius $R$ . Then $|D\setminus B_{R}|=|B_{R}\setminus D|$ . Since $|K_{BS}(z)|=(2\pi|z|)^{-1}$ by (a), $|K_{BS}|\leq(2\pi R)^{-1}$ on $D\setminus B_{R}$ and $|K_{BS}|>(2\pi R)^{-1}$ on $B_{R}\setminus D$ ; so $\int_{D}|K_{BS}|\leq\int_{B_{R}}|K_{BS}|=R$ , by (a). For fixed $y$ , the substitution $z=x-y$ maps $B_{R}$ onto the disk $D_{y}=\{z:|z+y|<R\}$ of radius $R$ , so Tonelli’s theorem gives $\int_{B_{R}}(|K_{BS}|\ast|g|)\differential x=\int|g(y)|\int_{D_{y}}|K_{BS}(z)|\differential z\differential y\leq R\|g\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}$ . Hence $|K_{BS}|\ast|g|$ is finite almost everywhere, and $K_{BS}\ast g\in L^{1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ because $|K_{BS}\ast g|\leq|K_{BS}|\ast|g|$ . Take $g_{n}\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ with $g_{n}\to g$ in $L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ . This bound, applied to $g_{n}-g$ , gives $K_{BS}\ast g_{n}\to K_{BS}\ast g$ in $L^{1}(B_{R})$ for every $R>0$ , hence in $\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ ; since $\divop(K_{BS}\ast g_{n})=0$ by (d), $\divop(K_{BS}\ast g)=0$ in $\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ . ∎

#### Lemma 2.2.

Let $4/3<p<\infty$ , $p^{\prime}=p/(p-1)$ , and $R>0$ . There is $C=C(p,R)$ such that the following hold.

- (a) For $\omega\in(L^{1}\cap L^{p})(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ the integral defining $K_{BS}\ast\omega$ converges absolutely almost everywhere and, with $v=K_{BS}\ast\omega$ ,

$$ \|v\|_{L^{p^{\prime}}(B_{R})}+\|v\|_{L^{2}(B_{R})}\leq C\|\omega\|_{(L^{1}\cap L^{p})(\mathbb{R}^{2})},\qquad\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}|\omega|\,\big(|K_{BS}|\ast|\omega|\big)\differential x\leq C\|\omega\|_{(L^{1}\cap L^{p})(\mathbb{R}^{2})}^{2}; $$

the constant in the second inequality can be chosen depending only on $p$ , independently of $R$ .

- (b) Let $\omega_{n}$ be real and $\omega_{n}\rightharpoonup\omega$ weakly in $L^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , with $\sup_{n}\|\omega_{n}\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\leq M$ . Then $\|\omega\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\leq M$ and $K_{BS}\ast\omega_{n}\to K_{BS}\ast\omega$ strongly in $L^{p^{\prime}}(B_{R})$ .

- (c) If $\omega\in(L^{1}\cap L^{2})(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , then $v=K_{BS}\ast\omega$ satisfies $\nabla v\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ and $\|\nabla v\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}=\|\omega\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}$ .

#### Proof.

(a) Put $r(p)=p^{\prime}$ and $s(p)=p/(2p-2)$ if $p\leq 2$ , and $r(p)=p$ and $s(p)=1$ if $p>2$ . Since $p>4/3$ , we have $s(p)\in[1,2)$ , so $K_{BS}^{\mathrm{nr}}\in L^{s(p)}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ . Moreover $1+1/r(p)=1/s(p)+1/p$ , so Young’s inequality gives $\||K_{BS}^{\mathrm{nr}}|\ast|\omega|\|_{L^{r(p)}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\leq\|K_{BS}^{\mathrm{nr}}\|_{L^{s(p)}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\|\omega\|_{L^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}$ . Also $\||K_{BS}^{\mathrm{fr}}|\ast|\omega|\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\leq\|\omega\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}/(2\pi)$ . Hence $|K_{BS}|\ast|\omega|$ is finite almost everywhere. Since $r(p)\geq\max\{2,p^{\prime}\}$ , Hölder’s inequality on $B_{R}$ gives the velocity bound. For the last bound, $r(p)^{\prime}\in[1,p]$ , so $\|\omega\|_{L^{r(p)^{\prime}}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\leq\|\omega\|_{(L^{1}\cap L^{p})(\mathbb{R}^{2})}$ by interpolation, and $\int|\omega|(|K_{BS}|\ast|\omega|)\leq\|\omega\|_{L^{r(p)^{\prime}}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\||K_{BS}^{\mathrm{nr}}|\ast|\omega|\|_{L^{r(p)}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}+\|\omega\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}^{2}/(2\pi)$ .

(b) For $L>0$ and $g\in L^{\infty}(B_{L})$ , the function $g\mathbf{1}_{B_{L}}$ lies in $L^{p^{\prime}}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , so $|\int_{B_{L}}\omega g|=\lim_{n}|\int_{B_{L}}\omega_{n}g|\leq M\|g\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}$ . The limit $\omega$ is real, as a weak limit of real functions. Taking $g=\sgn\omega$ (with $\sgn s=s/|s|$ for $s\neq 0$ and $\sgn 0=0$ ) and letting $L\to\infty$ gives $\|\omega\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\leq M$ .

By hypothesis and the bound just proved, $\omega_{n}$ and $\omega$ lie in $(L^{1}\cap L^{p})(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , with $L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ norms at most $M$ . Put $N=\sup_{n}\|\omega_{n}\|_{L^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}+\|\omega\|_{L^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}<\infty$ (weakly convergent sequences are bounded), let $0<\varepsilon<1<L$ , and split $K_{BS}=K^{(1)}+K^{(2)}+K^{(3)}$ with $K^{(1)}=K_{BS}\mathbf{1}_{B_{\varepsilon}}$ , $K^{(2)}=K_{BS}\mathbf{1}_{B_{L}\setminus B_{\varepsilon}}$ and $K^{(3)}=K_{BS}\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{R}^{2}\setminus B_{L}}$ . By Young’s inequality, as in (a), and Hölder’s inequality on $B_{R}$ , $\|K^{(1)}\ast(\omega_{n}-\omega)\|_{L^{p^{\prime}}(B_{R})}\leq|B_{R}|^{1/p^{\prime}-1/r(p)}\|K^{(1)}\|_{L^{s(p)}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}N$ , and $\|K^{(1)}\|_{L^{s(p)}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\to 0$ as $\varepsilon\to 0$ because $s(p)<2$ . Next, $|K^{(3)}\ast(\omega_{n}-\omega)|\leq 2M/(2\pi L)$ everywhere, since $\|\omega_{n}\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})},\|\omega\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\leq M$ ; so its $L^{p^{\prime}}(B_{R})$ norm is at most $|B_{R}|^{1/p^{\prime}}M/(\pi L)$ , uniformly in $n$ . Finally, for $x\in B_{R}$ the function $K^{(2)}(x-\cdot)$ is bounded by $(2\pi\varepsilon)^{-1}$ , since $|K_{BS}(z)|=(2\pi|z|)^{-1}$ and $|z|\geq\varepsilon$ on the support of $K^{(2)}$ , and vanishes outside $\{y:|x-y|<L\}$ ; hence it lies in $L^{p^{\prime}}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , so $K^{(2)}\ast\omega_{n}(x)\to K^{(2)}\ast\omega(x)$ , with $|K^{(2)}\ast\omega_{n}(x)|\leq\|K^{(2)}\|_{L^{p^{\prime}}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}N$ ; dominated convergence gives $K^{(2)}\ast\omega_{n}\to K^{(2)}\ast\omega$ in $L^{p^{\prime}}(B_{R})$ . Letting first $n\to\infty$ and then $\varepsilon\to 0$ and $L\to\infty$ gives (b).

(c) Choose $\omega_{j}\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ with $\omega_{j}\to\omega$ in $L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ and in $L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , and put $v_{j}=K_{BS}\ast\omega_{j}$ . By Lemma 2.1(d), applied to $\omega_{j}-\omega_{i}$ and to $\omega_{j}$ , $\|\nabla v_{j}-\nabla v_{i}\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}=\|\omega_{j}-\omega_{i}\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}$ and $\|\nabla v_{j}\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}=\|\omega_{j}\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}$ , so $\nabla v_{j}\to F$ in $L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ with $\|F\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}=\lim_{j}\|\omega_{j}\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}=\|\omega\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}$ . By Lemma 2.1(e), $v_{j}\to v$ in $L^{1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , so $\nabla v_{j}\to\nabla v$ in $\mathcal{D}^{\prime}$ , and $\nabla v=F$ . ∎

#### Definition 2.3.

Let $m\geq 1$ be an integer and let $g\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2};\mathbb{C})$ have compact support in $\mathbb{R}^{2}\setminus\{0\}$ . Writing $y\in\mathbb{R}^{2}$ as a complex number, we put

$$ p^{\mathrm{out}}_{m}[g]=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int g(y)\,(\bar{y})^{m}\differential y,\quad p^{\mathrm{in}}_{m}[g]=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int g(y)\,y^{-m}\differential y,\quad Q_{m}[g]=\int g(y)\,y^{m}\differential y. $$

These are the multipole moments of $g$ . In polar coordinates $y=se^{i\vartheta}$ , since $(\bar{y})^{m}=s^{m}e^{-im\vartheta}$ , $y^{-m}=s^{-m}e^{-im\vartheta}$ and $y^{m}=s^{m}e^{im\vartheta}$ , they read, with the angular modes $g_{\ell}$ of Section 2,

$$ p^{\mathrm{out}}_{m}[g]=\int_{0}^{\infty}g_{m}(s)\,s^{m+1}\differential s,\qquad p^{\mathrm{in}}_{m}[g]=\int_{0}^{\infty}g_{m}(s)\,s^{1-m}\differential s,\qquad Q_{m}[g]=2\pi\int_{0}^{\infty}g_{-m}(s)\,s^{m+1}\differential s; $$

so they see only the angular modes $\pm m$ of $g$ . Let $g$ be real with $\supp g\subset\{\rho_{1}\leq|y|\leq\rho_{2}\}$ , $0<\rho_{1}\leq\rho_{2}$ , and let $\psi(x)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int\log|x-y|\,g(y)\differential y$ be its stream function. Expanding $\log|x-y|=\log|x|+\real\log(1-y/x)$ for $|x|>\rho_{2}$ , and $\log|x-y|=\log|y|+\real\log(1-x/y)$ for $|x|<\rho_{1}$ , in powers of $y/x$ and $x/y$ gives

$$ \displaystyle\psi(x) \displaystyle=\frac{\int g}{2\pi}\log|x|-\real\sum_{m\geq 1}\frac{p^{\mathrm{out}}_{m}[g]}{m}(\bar{x})^{-m} \displaystyle(|x|>\rho_{2}), \displaystyle\psi(x) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int g(y)\log|y|\differential y-\real\sum_{m\geq 1}\frac{p^{\mathrm{in}}_{m}[g]}{m}\,x^{m} \displaystyle(|x|<\rho_{1}), $$

since $\overline{Q_{m}[g]}=2\pi p^{\mathrm{out}}_{m}[g]$ for real $g$ . Thus $p^{\mathrm{out}}_{m}[g]$ and $p^{\mathrm{in}}_{m}[g]$ give the field of $g$ in the angular modes $\pm m$ outside and inside its support.

### 2.3 Weak Solutions

#### Definition 2.4.

Two real functions $g,h\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ are equimeasurable if and only if $|\{g>s\}|=|\{h>s\}|$ and $|\{g<-s\}|=|\{h<-s\}|$ for every $s>0$ .

#### Definition 2.5.

Let $4/3<q<\infty$ , $T>0$ and $\omega^{\mathrm{in}}\in(L^{1}\cap L^{q})(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ . A weak solution with datum $\omega^{\mathrm{in}}$ in $X_{q}(T)$ is a function $\omega\in X_{q}(T)$ such that, with $v(t)=K_{BS}\ast\omega(t)$ ,

$$ \int_{0}^{T}\!\!\int\omega\,(\partial_{t}\varphi+v\cdot\nabla\varphi)\differential x\differential t+\int\omega^{\mathrm{in}}\varphi(0,\cdot)\differential x=0\qquad\text{for all }\varphi\in\mathcal{D}_{T}. $$

It is renormalized if and only if, in addition, for every $\Upsilon\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R})$ with $\Upsilon^{\prime}$ bounded and $\Upsilon(0)=0$ ,

$$ \int_{0}^{T}\!\!\int\Upsilon(\omega)\,(\partial_{t}\varphi+v\cdot\nabla\varphi)\differential x\differential t+\int\Upsilon(\omega^{\mathrm{in}})\varphi(0,\cdot)\differential x=0\qquad\text{for all }\varphi\in\mathcal{D}_{T}. $$

For $T_{0}\in(0,\infty]$ , a (renormalized) weak solution on $[0,T_{0})$ is a function on $[0,T_{0})$ whose restriction to $[0,T)$ is a (renormalized) weak solution in $X_{q}(T)$ for every $T<T_{0}$ .

The integrals in Equations (4) and (5) converge absolutely, because $|\Upsilon(\omega)|\leq\|\Upsilon^{\prime}\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R})}|\omega|$ and $|\omega v|\leq|\omega|(|K_{BS}|\ast|\omega|)$ , and Lemma 2.2(a), with $p=q$ and $R=1$ , gives $\|\omega(t)v(t)\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\leq C(q,1)\operatorname{ess\,sup}_{0<s<T}\|\omega(s)\|_{(L^{1}\cap L^{q})(\mathbb{R}^{2})}^{2}$ for almost every $t\in(0,T)$ .

## 3 Compactness and a Non-Uniqueness Criterion

Compactness results for sequences of renormalized solutions go back to DiPerna and Lions [10]; we give a self-contained proof of the one we need. We prove it only for vorticity in $L^{\infty}_{t}(L^{1}\cap L^{2})_{x}$ , which is all that the proof of Theorem 1.1 needs. The arguments control $\nabla v$ by $\omega$ : for vorticity in $L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ this is the identity $\|\nabla v\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}=\|\omega\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}$ of Lemma 2.2(c), while for vorticity in $L^{q}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , $q\neq 2$ , it would require the $L^{q}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ bounds of the Calderón-Zygmund (Riesz transform) estimate. Equations (4) and (5) do not involve $q$ , so, for $q\in(4/3,\infty)$ , a renormalized weak solution in $X_{2}(T)$ that lies in $X_{q}(T)$ , with datum in $(L^{1}\cap L^{q})(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , is a renormalized weak solution in $X_{q}(T)$ ; Theorem 3.8(ii) gives this membership.

All functions in this section are real valued, except $\Psi$ in Corollary 3.9. Let $\varsigma\in C_{c}^{\infty}(B_{2})$ with $0\leq\varsigma\leq 1$ and $\varsigma=1$ on $B_{1}$ , and put $\varsigma_{R}=\varsigma(\cdot/R)$ , so that $|\nabla\varsigma_{R}|\leq\|\nabla\varsigma\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}/R$ . Let $\rho\in C_{c}^{\infty}(B_{1})$ and $\rho^{\mathrm{t}}\in C_{c}^{\infty}((-1,1))$ be nonnegative with integral $1$ , and put $\rho_{\varepsilon}=\varepsilon^{-2}\rho(\cdot/\varepsilon)$ and $\rho^{\mathrm{t}}_{\delta}=\delta^{-1}\rho^{\mathrm{t}}(\cdot/\delta)$ ; convolution with $\rho_{\varepsilon}$ acts in the space variable only, and convolution with $\rho^{\mathrm{t}}_{\delta}$ in the time variable only. Let $\varkappa\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R})$ be nondecreasing with $\varkappa=0$ on $(-\infty,0]$ and $\varkappa=1$ on $[1,\infty)$ . We write $C_{\mathrm{v}}$ for the constant $C(2,1)$ of Lemma 2.2(a); thus $\int|g|(|K_{BS}|\ast|g|)\differential x\leq C_{\mathrm{v}}\|g\|_{(L^{1}\cap L^{2})(\mathbb{R}^{2})}^{2}$ for $g\in(L^{1}\cap L^{2})(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ .

### 3.1 The Linear Transport Equation

Let $T>0$ and $t_{0}\in[0,T)$ , let $w$ be a real measurable vector field and $u$ a real measurable function on $(t_{0},T)\times\mathbb{R}^{2}$ , and let $u_{0}\in L^{1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ be real, such that $u$ , $w$ and $uw$ are integrable on $(t_{0},T^{\prime})\times B_{R}$ for all $T^{\prime}<T$ and $R>0$ . We say that $u$ satisfies Equation (6) on $[t_{0},T)$ with field $w$ and datum $u_{0}$ if

$$ \int_{t_{0}}^{T}\!\!\int u\,(\partial_{t}\varphi+w\cdot\nabla\varphi)\differential x\differential t+\int u_{0}\,\varphi(t_{0},\cdot)\differential x=0\qquad\text{for all }\varphi\in\mathcal{D}_{T}; $$

every integral here converges. Thus $\omega\in X_{2}(T)$ is a weak solution of the Euler equations with datum $\omega^{\mathrm{in}}\in(L^{1}\cap L^{2})(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ if and only if it satisfies Equation (6) on $[0,T)$ with field $v=K_{BS}\ast\omega$ and datum $\omega^{\mathrm{in}}$ , and it is renormalized if and only if, in addition, $\Upsilon(\omega)$ satisfies Equation (6) on $[0,T)$ with field $v$ and datum $\Upsilon(\omega^{\mathrm{in}})$ for every $\Upsilon\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R})$ with $\Upsilon^{\prime}$ bounded and $\Upsilon(0)=0$ . The integrability conditions hold by Lemma 2.2(a).

#### Lemma 3.1.

Let $t_{0}<T$ , $B\in L^{\infty}(t_{0},T)$ and $b_{0}\in\mathbb{R}$ , and suppose that, for every $\alpha\in C_{c}^{\infty}((-\infty,T))$ , $\int_{t_{0}}^{T}\alpha^{\prime}(t)B(t)\differential t+\alpha(t_{0})b_{0}=0$ . Then $B=b_{0}$ almost everywhere on $(t_{0},T)$ .

#### Proof.

For $0<\delta<(T-t_{0})/2$ and $t\in(t_{0}+\delta,T-\delta)$ put $B_{\delta}(t)=\int B(s)\rho^{\mathrm{t}}_{\delta}(t-s)\differential s$ . The function $\alpha(s)=\rho^{\mathrm{t}}_{\delta}(t-s)$ vanishes outside $(t-\delta,t+\delta)$ , which lies in $(t_{0},T)$ because $t-t_{0}>\delta$ and $T-t>\delta$ ; so $\alpha\in C_{c}^{\infty}((t_{0},T))$ and $\alpha(t_{0})=0$ , and the hypothesis gives $B_{\delta}^{\prime}(t)=-\int B(s)\,\partial_{s}\big(\rho^{\mathrm{t}}_{\delta}(t-s)\big)\differential s=0$ , so $B_{\delta}$ is constant on $(t_{0}+\delta,T-\delta)$ . Since $B_{\delta}\to B$ in $L^{1}_{\mathrm{loc}}((t_{0},T))$ as $\delta\to 0$ , the constants converge to some $c\in\mathbb{R}$ and $B=c$ almost everywhere. For $\alpha$ with $\alpha(t_{0})=1$ we have $\int_{t_{0}}^{T}\alpha^{\prime}c\differential t=-c$ , because $\alpha$ vanishes near $T$ ; so the hypothesis gives $b_{0}=c$ . ∎

#### Lemma 3.2.

Let $T>0$ . Let $w$ be a vector field with $w\in L^{\infty}(0,T;L^{2}(B_{R}))$ for every $R>0$ , let $u\in L^{\infty}(0,T;L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2}))$ and $u_{0}\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , and suppose that $u$ satisfies Equation (6) on $[0,T)$ with field $w$ and datum $u_{0}$ . Put $N=\operatorname{ess\,sup}_{t}\|u(t)\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}$ . Then $u$ has a representative $\tilde{u}\colon[0,T]\to L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ with the following properties.

- (a) $\tilde{u}$ is weakly continuous, $\tilde{u}(0)=u_{0}$ , and $\|\tilde{u}(t)\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\leq N$ for every $t$ . If also $u\in L^{\infty}(0,T;L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2}))$ , then $\|\tilde{u}(t)\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\leq\operatorname{ess\,sup}_{s}\|u(s)\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}$ for every $t$ .

- (b) For $\psi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ with $\supp\psi\subset B_{R}$ and every $t\in[0,T]$ , $\int\tilde{u}(t)\psi=\int u_{0}\psi+\int_{0}^{t}\!\int u\,w\cdot\nabla\psi$ . In particular, for $s,t\in[0,T]$ ,

$$ \Big|\int(\tilde{u}(t)-\tilde{u}(s))\psi\Big|\leq N\,\|w\|_{L^{\infty}(0,T;L^{2}(B_{R}))}\|\nabla\psi\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}|t-s|. $$

- (c) For every $t_{0}\in[0,T)$ , $u$ satisfies Equation (6) on $[t_{0},T)$ with field $w$ and datum $\tilde{u}(t_{0})$ .

#### Proof.

For $j\in\mathbb{N}$ , $C_{c}^{\infty}(B_{j})$ is a subset of the separable Banach space $C^{1}(\overline{B_{j}})$ , hence separable: there is a countable set $\mathcal{F}_{j}\subset C_{c}^{\infty}(B_{j})$ such that every $\psi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(B_{j})$ is the limit in $C^{1}$ of elements of $\mathcal{F}_{j}$ . The countable union $\mathcal{F}=\bigcup_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\mathcal{F}_{j}\subset C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ does not depend on $j$ , and every $\psi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(B_{j})$ , $j\in\mathbb{N}$ , is the limit in $C^{1}$ of elements of $\mathcal{F}\cap C_{c}^{\infty}(B_{j})$ . $C_{c}^{\infty}$ is dense in $L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , and convergence in $C^{1}$ with supports in a fixed $B_{j}$ implies convergence in $L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ ; so $\mathcal{F}$ is dense in $L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ . Write $W_{R}=\|w\|_{L^{\infty}(0,T;L^{2}(B_{R}))}$ .

For $\psi\in\mathcal{F}$ with $\supp\psi\subset B_{R}$ put $a_{\psi}(t)=\int u(t)\psi$ and $c_{\psi}(t)=\int u(t)\,w(t)\cdot\nabla\psi$ . These are measurable by Fubini’s theorem, and $|c_{\psi}|\leq NW_{R}\|\nabla\psi\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}$ almost everywhere by Hölder’s inequality, so $A_{\psi}(t)=\int u_{0}\psi+\int_{0}^{t}c_{\psi}$ is Lipschitz on $[0,T]$ . For $\alpha\in C_{c}^{\infty}((-\infty,T))$ , Equation (6) with the test function $\alpha(t)\psi(x)$ gives $\int_{0}^{T}\alpha^{\prime}a_{\psi}+\int_{0}^{T}\alpha c_{\psi}+\alpha(0)\int u_{0}\psi=0$ . Since $\alpha$ vanishes near $T$ and $A_{\psi}^{\prime}=c_{\psi}$ almost everywhere, integration by parts gives $\int_{0}^{T}\alpha c_{\psi}=-\int_{0}^{T}\alpha^{\prime}A_{\psi}-\alpha(0)\int u_{0}\psi$ . Hence $\int_{0}^{T}\alpha^{\prime}(a_{\psi}-A_{\psi})=0$ , and Lemma 3.1, with $t_{0}=0$ and $b_{0}=0$ , gives $a_{\psi}=A_{\psi}$ almost everywhere. Let $\mathcal{N}$ be the union of $\{0,T\}$ , of the exceptional null sets of these identities for $\psi\in\mathcal{F}$ , of the set of $t$ with $u(t)\notin L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ or $\|u(t)\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}>N$ , and, if $u\in L^{\infty}(0,T;L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2}))$ , of the set of $t$ with $\|u(t)\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}>N_{1}:=\operatorname{ess\,sup}_{s}\|u(s)\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}$ . As $\mathcal{F}$ is countable, $\mathcal{N}$ is a null set.

For $t\notin\mathcal{N}$ put $\tilde{u}(t)=u(t)$ . For $t\in\mathcal{N}$ take $t_{j}\notin\mathcal{N}$ with $t_{j}\to t$ . Then $\|u(t_{j})\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\leq N$ and $\int u(t_{j})\psi=A_{\psi}(t_{j})\to A_{\psi}(t)$ for $\psi\in\mathcal{F}$ . Since $\mathcal{F}$ is dense in $L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , $\int u(t_{j})\phi$ converges for every $\phi\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , to a linear functional of norm at most $N$ ; by the Riesz representation theorem in $L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , it is $\phi\mapsto\int\tilde{u}(t)\phi$ for a unique $\tilde{u}(t)\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , which does not depend on the sequence, because $\int\tilde{u}(t)\psi=A_{\psi}(t)$ for $\psi\in\mathcal{F}$ . Thus $\tilde{u}=u$ almost everywhere, $\|\tilde{u}(t)\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\leq N$ for every $t$ , and $\int\tilde{u}(t)\psi=A_{\psi}(t)$ for all $t\in[0,T]$ and $\psi\in\mathcal{F}$ .

We prove (a) and (b). For $\phi\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , $\psi\in\mathcal{F}$ and $s,t\in[0,T]$ , $|\int(\tilde{u}(t)-\tilde{u}(s))\phi|\leq 2N\|\phi-\psi\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}+|A_{\psi}(t)-A_{\psi}(s)|$ . Given $\phi$ and $\eta>0$ , first choose $\psi\in\mathcal{F}$ with $2N\|\phi-\psi\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}<\eta/2$ , which is possible as $\mathcal{F}$ is dense in $L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ ; then, since $A_{\psi}$ is Lipschitz, $|A_{\psi}(t)-A_{\psi}(s)|<\eta/2$ whenever $|t-s|$ is small enough. So $t\mapsto\int\tilde{u}(t)\phi$ is continuous for every $\phi\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , that is, $\tilde{u}$ is weakly continuous; and $\tilde{u}(0)=u_{0}$ , because $A_{\psi}(0)=\int u_{0}\psi$ . If $u\in L^{\infty}(0,T;L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2}))$ and $t\in\mathcal{N}$ , then $u(t_{j})\rightharpoonup\tilde{u}(t)$ weakly in $L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ and $\|u(t_{j})\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\leq N_{1}$ , so $\|\tilde{u}(t)\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\leq N_{1}$ by Lemma 2.2(b) with $p=2$ . For (b), let $\psi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(B_{j})$ and $\psi_{i}\in\mathcal{F}\cap C_{c}^{\infty}(B_{j})$ with $\psi_{i}\to\psi$ in $C^{1}$ . Then $\int\tilde{u}(t)\psi_{i}\to\int\tilde{u}(t)\psi$ , since $\|\psi_{i}-\psi\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\leq|B_{j}|^{1/2}\|\psi_{i}-\psi\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}$ , and $A_{\psi_{i}}(t)\to\int u_{0}\psi+\int_{0}^{t}\!\int u\,w\cdot\nabla\psi$ , since $\int u_{0}\psi_{i}\to\int u_{0}\psi$ and $|\int_{0}^{t}\!\int u\,w\cdot\nabla(\psi_{i}-\psi)|\leq TNW_{j}\|\nabla(\psi_{i}-\psi)\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}$ . This is the identity in (b), and the bound on $c_{\psi}$ gives the Lipschitz bound.

For (c), the case $t_{0}=0$ is the hypothesis, since $\tilde{u}(0)=u_{0}$ . Let $t_{0}\in(0,T)$ and $\varphi\in\mathcal{D}_{T}$ , and for $0<h<T-t_{0}$ put $\varkappa_{h}(t)=\varkappa((t-t_{0})/h)$ . Equation (6) with the test function $\varkappa_{h}\varphi\in\mathcal{D}_{T}$ , which vanishes for $t\leq t_{0}$ , gives

$$ \int_{0}^{T}\!\!\int\varkappa_{h}\,u\,(\partial_{t}\varphi+w\cdot\nabla\varphi)\differential x\differential t+\int_{0}^{T}\varkappa_{h}^{\prime}(t)\,g(t)\differential t=0,\qquad g(t)=\int\tilde{u}(t)\varphi(t)\differential x. $$

The function $g$ is continuous, since $|g(t)-g(s)|\leq N\|\varphi(t)-\varphi(s)\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}+|\int(\tilde{u}(t)-\tilde{u}(s))\varphi(s)|$ and $\tilde{u}$ is weakly continuous. As $h\to 0$ , the second term tends to $g(t_{0})$ : since $\varkappa_{h}^{\prime}\geq 0$ , $\int\varkappa_{h}^{\prime}=1$ and $\supp\varkappa_{h}^{\prime}\subset[t_{0},t_{0}+h]$ , the functions $\varkappa_{h}^{\prime}$ converge to the Dirac mass at $t_{0}$ in the sense of distributions, indeed against every continuous function, and $g$ is continuous; and, since $\varkappa_{h}\to\mathbf{1}_{(t_{0},\infty)}$ pointwise, the first term tends to $\int_{t_{0}}^{T}\!\int u\,(\partial_{t}\varphi+w\cdot\nabla\varphi)$ by dominated convergence, with the integrable dominating function $|u|(|\partial_{t}\varphi|+|w||\nabla\varphi|)$ . This is (c). ∎

### 3.2 Weakly Continuous Representatives

Let $\omega$ be a weak solution in $X_{2}(T)$ with datum $\omega^{\mathrm{in}}$ , and put $v=K_{BS}\ast\omega$ . By Lemma 2.2(a), $g\mapsto K_{BS}\ast g$ is linear and bounded from $(L^{1}\cap L^{2})(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ to $L^{2}(B_{R})$ , and such a map preserves strong measurability; so $v\in L^{\infty}(0,T;L^{2}(B_{R}))$ for every $R>0$ , and $\|\omega(t)v(t)\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\leq C_{\mathrm{v}}\|\omega(t)\|_{(L^{1}\cap L^{2})(\mathbb{R}^{2})}^{2}$ for almost every $t$ , so $\omega v\in L^{1}((0,T)\times\mathbb{R}^{2})$ . Hence Lemma 3.2 applies with $u=\omega$ , $w=v$ and $u_{0}=\omega^{\mathrm{in}}$ . From now on every such weak solution is identified with its weakly continuous representative, so that $\omega(t)$ is defined for every $t\in[0,T]$ , $\omega(0)=\omega^{\mathrm{in}}$ , and $\|\omega(t)\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}$ and $\|\omega(t)\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}$ are bounded by the corresponding essential suprema for every $t$ . Two weakly continuous functions that agree for almost every $t$ agree for every $t$ ; hence the representatives on the intervals $[0,T]$ , $T<T_{0}$ , of a weak solution on $[0,T_{0})$ with $q=2$ define a weakly continuous representative on $[0,T_{0})$ . Moreover $\|\nabla v(t)\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}=\|\omega(t)\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}$ by Lemma 2.2(c) and $\divop v(t)=0$ by Lemma 2.1(e); thus $v\in L^{\infty}(0,T;W^{1,2}(B_{R}))$ for every $R>0$ , and $v$ is divergence-free.

### 3.3 Renormalization

For an open interval $I$ , a vector field $w$ and a function $u$ on $I\times\mathbb{R}^{2}$ with $u,wu\in L^{1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(I\times\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , put

$$ C_{\varepsilon}[u,w]=w\cdot\nabla(u\ast\rho_{\varepsilon})-\big(\divop(wu)\big)\ast\rho_{\varepsilon}, $$

where $\big(\divop(wu)\big)\ast\rho_{\varepsilon}(t,x)=\int(wu)(t,y)\cdot\nabla\rho_{\varepsilon}(x-y)\differential y$ . Both terms of $C_{\varepsilon}$ are defined by these formulas, not derived: the divergence $\divop(wu)$ is a distribution, and its convolution in $x$ with $\rho_{\varepsilon}$ , which acts by pairing it with $\rho_{\varepsilon}(x-\cdot)$ , is the function displayed above, since $wu\in L^{1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(I\times\mathbb{R}^{2})$ . The function $u\ast\rho_{\varepsilon}(t,\cdot)$ is smooth, and $w\cdot\nabla(u\ast\rho_{\varepsilon})$ is its pointwise product with $w$ . Writing $w(t,x)\cdot\nabla(u\ast\rho_{\varepsilon})(t,x)=\int u(t,y)\,w(t,x)\cdot\nabla\rho_{\varepsilon}(x-y)\differential y$ and substituting $y=x-\varepsilon z$ , we get, for almost every $(t,x)$ ,

$$ \displaystyle C_{\varepsilon}[u,w](t,x) \displaystyle=\int u(t,y)\,\big(w(t,x)-w(t,y)\big)\cdot\nabla\rho_{\varepsilon}(x-y)\differential y \displaystyle=\int_{B_{1}}u(t,x-\varepsilon z)\,\frac{w(t,x)-w(t,x-\varepsilon z)}{\varepsilon}\cdot\nabla\rho(z)\differential z, $$

because $\nabla\rho_{\varepsilon}(\varepsilon z)=\varepsilon^{-3}\nabla\rho(z)$ . The map $(u,w)\mapsto C_{\varepsilon}[u,w]$ is bilinear.

#### Lemma 3.3 (cf. Lemma II.1 in [10]).

Let $I\subset\mathbb{R}$ be an open interval, let $w\in L^{1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(I;W^{1,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{2};\mathbb{R}^{2}))$ with $\divop w=0$ , and let $u\in L^{\infty}_{\mathrm{loc}}(I;L^{2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{2}))$ . Then $C_{\varepsilon}[u,w]\to 0$ in $L^{1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(I\times\mathbb{R}^{2})$ as $\varepsilon\to 0$ .

#### Proof.

Note that $wu\in L^{1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(I\times\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality in $x$ . Fix a compact interval $J\subset I$ and $R>0$ , and write $\|\cdot\|_{q,r}$ for the norm of $L^{q}(B_{r})$ .

We first prove a bound that is uniform in $\varepsilon\in(0,1]$ and does not use $\divop w=0$ . If $w(t,\cdot)\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2};\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , then $w(x)-w(x-\varepsilon z)=\varepsilon\int_{0}^{1}\nabla w(x-s\varepsilon z)z\differential s$ , and Equation (7) with $|z|\leq 1$ and the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality in $x$ give

$$ \displaystyle\|C_{\varepsilon}[u,w](t)\|_{1,R} \displaystyle\leq\|\nabla\rho\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\int_{B_{1}}\!\int_{0}^{1}\!\int_{B_{R}}|u(t,x-\varepsilon z)|\,|\nabla w(t,x-s\varepsilon z)|\differential x\differential s\differential z \displaystyle\leq\pi\|\nabla\rho\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\|u(t)\|_{2,R+1}\|\nabla w(t)\|_{2,R+1}. $$

For general $w$ , apply this to $w_{\delta}=w\ast\rho_{\delta}$ , $\delta\in(0,1]$ , for which $\|\nabla w_{\delta}(t)\|_{2,R+1}\leq\|\nabla w(t)\|_{2,R+2}$ by Young’s inequality. For fixed $\varepsilon$ , the first line of Equation (7) and the inequalities of Hölder and Young, with $\|\nabla\rho_{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}=\varepsilon^{-1}\|\nabla\rho\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}$ , give

$$ \|C_{\varepsilon}[u,w-w_{\delta}](t)\|_{1,R}\leq 2\varepsilon^{-1}\|\nabla\rho\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\|u(t)\|_{2,R+1}\|(w-w_{\delta})(t)\|_{2,R+1}, $$

which tends to $0$ as $\delta\to 0$ for almost every $t$ , because mollification converges in $L^{2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ . Hence, for almost every $t\in J$ and all $\varepsilon\in(0,1]$ ,

$$ \|C_{\varepsilon}[u,w](t)\|_{1,R}\leq C_{\rho}\,\|u(t)\|_{2,R+1}\,\|\nabla w(t)\|_{2,R+2},\qquad C_{\rho}=\pi\|\nabla\rho\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}. $$

We now use $\divop w=0$ . For $\delta\in(0,1]$ put $u_{\delta}(t)=u(t)\ast\rho_{\delta}$ . For almost every $t\in J$ , $u_{\delta}(t)$ is smooth with $\|\nabla u_{\delta}(t)\|_{\infty,R+1}\leq\|\nabla\rho_{\delta}\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\|u(t)\|_{1,R+2}$ , and, for $\phi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , $\int wu_{\delta}\cdot\nabla\phi=\int w\cdot\nabla(u_{\delta}\phi)-\int\phi\,w\cdot\nabla u_{\delta}=-\int\phi\,w\cdot\nabla u_{\delta}$ , because $\divop w(t)=0$ . Thus $\divop(wu_{\delta})=w\cdot\nabla u_{\delta}$ , and

$$ C_{\varepsilon}[u_{\delta},w]=w\cdot\big((\nabla u_{\delta})\ast\rho_{\varepsilon}-\nabla u_{\delta}\big)+\big(w\cdot\nabla u_{\delta}-(w\cdot\nabla u_{\delta})\ast\rho_{\varepsilon}\big). $$

As $\varepsilon\to 0$ , for almost every $t\in J$ the first term tends to $0$ in $L^{1}(B_{R})$ , because $\nabla u_{\delta}(t)$ is uniformly continuous on $\overline{B_{R+1}}$ , and so does the second, because $w\cdot\nabla u_{\delta}(t)\in L^{1}(B_{R+1})$ . Since $\|C_{\varepsilon}[u_{\delta},w](t)\|_{1,R}\leq 4\|w(t)\|_{1,R+1}\|\nabla u_{\delta}(t)\|_{\infty,R+1}$ , which is integrable on $J$ because $w\in L^{1}(J;L^{1}(B_{R+1}))$ and $u\in L^{\infty}(J;L^{1}(B_{R+2}))$ , $C_{\varepsilon}[u_{\delta},w]\to 0$ in $L^{1}(J\times B_{R})$ for each $\delta$ . Finally, by bilinearity and Equation (8),

$$ \sup_{\varepsilon\leq 1}\|C_{\varepsilon}[u,w]-C_{\varepsilon}[u_{\delta},w]\|_{L^{1}(J\times B_{R})}\leq C_{\rho}\int_{J}\|(u-u_{\delta})(t)\|_{2,R+1}\|\nabla w(t)\|_{2,R+2}\differential t, $$

Call the right side $\eta(\delta)$ ; it does not depend on $\varepsilon$ , and $\eta(\delta)\to 0$ as $\delta\to 0$ by dominated convergence, since $\|(u-u_{\delta})(t)\|_{2,R+1}\to 0$ for almost every $t$ and is at most $2\|u\|_{L^{\infty}(J;L^{2}(B_{R+2}))}$ . Thus $\|C_{\varepsilon}[u,w]\|_{L^{1}(J\times B_{R})}\leq\|C_{\varepsilon}[u_{\delta},w]\|_{L^{1}(J\times B_{R})}+\eta(\delta)$ for all $\varepsilon\in(0,1]$ and $\delta\in(0,1]$ . Letting first $\varepsilon\to 0$ with $\delta$ fixed gives $\limsup_{\varepsilon\to 0}\|C_{\varepsilon}[u,w]\|_{L^{1}(J\times B_{R})}\leq\eta(\delta)$ , and letting then $\delta\to 0$ gives $C_{\varepsilon}[u,w]\to 0$ in $L^{1}(J\times B_{R})$ . ∎

#### Lemma 3.4.

Let $T>0$ and $t_{0}\in[0,T)$ . Let $w\in L^{\infty}(0,T;W^{1,2}_{\mathrm{loc}})$ with $\divop w=0$ , let $u\in X_{2}(T)$ with $uw\in L^{1}((0,T)\times\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , and let $u_{0}\in(L^{1}\cap L^{2})(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ . Assume that $u$ satisfies Equation (6) on $[t_{0},T)$ with field $w$ and datum $u_{0}$ . Then, for every $\Upsilon\in\mathrm{Lip}_{0}$ :

- (i) $\Upsilon(u)$ satisfies Equation (6) on $[t_{0},T)$ with field $w$ and datum $\Upsilon(u_{0})$ ;

- (ii) $\int\Upsilon(u(t))\differential x=\int\Upsilon(u_{0})\differential x$ for almost every $t\in(t_{0},T)$ .

#### Proof.

We first prove (i) for $\Upsilon\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R})$ with $|\Upsilon^{\prime}|\leq L$ and $\Upsilon(0)=0$ . Put $I=(t_{0}-1,T)$ , and redefine $w$ and $u$ on $(t_{0}-1,t_{0}]$ by $w=0$ and $u=u_{0}$ ; on $(t_{0},T)$ they are unchanged. For $\varphi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(I\times\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , extended by zero to an element of $\mathcal{D}_{T}$ , the interval $(t_{0}-1,t_{0})$ contributes $\int_{t_{0}-1}^{t_{0}}\!\int u_{0}\partial_{t}\varphi=\int u_{0}\varphi(t_{0})$ to $\int_{I}\!\int u(\partial_{t}\varphi+w\cdot\nabla\varphi)$ , and by Equation (6) the interval $(t_{0},T)$ contributes $-\int u_{0}\varphi(t_{0})$ . Thus $\partial_{t}u+\divop(wu)=0$ in $\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(I\times\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , and the extended pair satisfies the hypotheses of Lemma 3.3 on $I$ .

Let $u_{\varepsilon}=u\ast\rho_{\varepsilon}$ . Then $\nabla u_{\varepsilon}\in L^{\infty}_{\mathrm{loc}}(I\times\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , and convolving the equation $\partial_{t}u+\divop(wu)=0$ in $x$ with $\rho_{\varepsilon}$ gives $\partial_{t}u_{\varepsilon}=-\big(\divop(wu)\big)\ast\rho_{\varepsilon}\in L^{1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(I\times\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , where, as $wu\in L^{1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(I\times\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , the right side is the function defined at the start of this subsection, so $u_{\varepsilon}\in W^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(I\times\mathbb{R}^{2})$ and $\partial_{t}u_{\varepsilon}+w\cdot\nabla u_{\varepsilon}=C_{\varepsilon}[u,w]$ . For almost every $t$ , $\Upsilon(u_{\varepsilon}(t))$ is a $C^{1}$ function of $x$ with locally bounded gradient, so $\divop\big(w\Upsilon(u_{\varepsilon})\big)=w\cdot\nabla\Upsilon(u_{\varepsilon})$ because $\divop w=0$ ; with the chain rule in $W^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ this gives

$$ \partial_{t}\Upsilon(u_{\varepsilon})+\divop\big(w\Upsilon(u_{\varepsilon})\big)=\Upsilon^{\prime}(u_{\varepsilon})C_{\varepsilon}[u,w]\qquad\text{in }\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(I\times\mathbb{R}^{2}). $$

As $\varepsilon\to 0$ , the right side tends to $0$ in $L^{1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(I\times\mathbb{R}^{2})$ by Lemma 3.3, since $|\Upsilon^{\prime}|\leq L$ . For almost every $t$ , $u_{\varepsilon}(t)\to u(t)$ in $L^{2}(B_{R})$ , with the bound $2\|u\|_{L^{\infty}(I;L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2}))}$ ; since $|\Upsilon(u_{\varepsilon})-\Upsilon(u)|\leq L|u_{\varepsilon}-u|$ and $w\in L^{\infty}(I;L^{2}(B_{R}))$ , dominated convergence gives $\Upsilon(u_{\varepsilon})\to\Upsilon(u)$ and $w\Upsilon(u_{\varepsilon})\to w\Upsilon(u)$ in $L^{1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(I\times\mathbb{R}^{2})$ . Therefore $\partial_{t}\Upsilon(u)+\divop\big(w\Upsilon(u)\big)=0$ in $\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(I\times\mathbb{R}^{2})$ . Now let $\varphi\in\mathcal{D}_{T}$ and $\kappa_{0}(t)=\varkappa\big(3(t-t_{0})+2\big)$ , so that $\kappa_{0}=0$ on $(-\infty,t_{0}-2/3]$ and $\kappa_{0}=1$ on $[t_{0}-1/3,\infty)$ . Test the last equation with $\kappa_{0}\varphi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(I\times\mathbb{R}^{2})$ . On $(t_{0}-1,t_{0})$ , $w=0$ and $\Upsilon(u)=\Upsilon(u_{0})$ , so this interval contributes $\int_{t_{0}-1}^{t_{0}}\!\int\Upsilon(u_{0})\partial_{t}(\kappa_{0}\varphi)=\int\Upsilon(u_{0})\varphi(t_{0})$ , while $\kappa_{0}=1$ on $(t_{0},T)$ . This is (i) for $\Upsilon$ .

Let now $\Upsilon\in\mathrm{Lip}_{0}$ have Lipschitz constant $L$ , and put $\Upsilon_{j}=\Upsilon\ast\rho^{\mathrm{t}}_{1/j}-(\Upsilon\ast\rho^{\mathrm{t}}_{1/j})(0)$ . Then $\Upsilon_{j}\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R})$ , $|\Upsilon_{j}^{\prime}|\leq L$ , $\Upsilon_{j}(0)=0$ , and $|\Upsilon_{j}-\Upsilon|\leq 2L/j$ , because $|\Upsilon\ast\rho^{\mathrm{t}}_{1/j}-\Upsilon|\leq L/j$ and $\Upsilon(0)=0$ . Since $|\Upsilon(u)|\leq L|u|$ , all integrals in Equation (6) for $\Upsilon(u)$ converge. For $\varphi\in\mathcal{D}_{T}$ with $\supp\varphi\subset(-\infty,T^{\prime}]\times B_{R}$ , $T^{\prime}<T$ , the left sides of Equation (6) for $\Upsilon_{j}(u)$ (which vanish) and for $\Upsilon(u)$ differ by at most $\frac{2L}{j}\big(\int_{t_{0}}^{T^{\prime}}\!\int_{B_{R}}(|\partial_{t}\varphi|+|w||\nabla\varphi|)+\int_{B_{R}}|\varphi(t_{0})|\big)$ , which tends to $0$ because $w$ is integrable on $(t_{0},T^{\prime})\times B_{R}$ . This proves (i).

For (ii), let $\Upsilon\in\mathrm{Lip}_{0}$ have Lipschitz constant $L$ , and let $\alpha\in C_{c}^{\infty}((-\infty,T))$ . Since $\Upsilon(u)$ solves Equation (6) by (i), we test it against $\alpha(t)\varsigma_{R}(x)$ and get

$$ \int_{t_{0}}^{T}\alpha^{\prime}(t)\Big(\int\Upsilon(u(t))\varsigma_{R}\differential x\Big)\differential t+\alpha(t_{0})\int\Upsilon(u_{0})\varsigma_{R}\differential x=-\int_{t_{0}}^{T}\alpha(t)\int\Upsilon(u)\,w\cdot\nabla\varsigma_{R}\differential x\differential t, $$

whose right side is at most $\|\alpha\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R})}L\|\nabla\varsigma\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}R^{-1}\|uw\|_{L^{1}((0,T)\times\mathbb{R}^{2})}$ . As $R\to\infty$ , dominated convergence, with $|\Upsilon(u)|\leq L|u|$ and $u\in L^{\infty}(0,T;L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2}))$ , gives $\int_{t_{0}}^{T}\alpha^{\prime}B+\alpha(t_{0})b_{0}=0$ with $B(t)=\int\Upsilon(u(t))$ , a measurable function bounded by $L\|u\|_{L^{\infty}(0,T;L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2}))}$ , and $b_{0}=\int\Upsilon(u_{0})$ . Lemma 3.1 gives (ii). ∎

#### Lemma 3.5.

Let $T>0$ and let $\omega$ be a renormalized weak solution of the Euler equations in $X_{2}(T)$ with datum $\omega^{\mathrm{in}}$ . Then for every $t\in[0,T)$ and every $\Upsilon\in\mathrm{Lip}_{0}$ ,

$$ \int\Upsilon(\omega(t))\differential x=\int\Upsilon(\omega^{\mathrm{in}})\differential x. $$

Consequently, for every $t\in[0,T)$ , $\|\omega(t)\|_{L^{q}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}=\|\omega^{\mathrm{in}}\|_{L^{q}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}$ for every $q\in[1,2]$ , and $\omega(t)$ is equimeasurable with $\omega^{\mathrm{in}}$ . Moreover $\omega\in C([0,T);L^{q}(\mathbb{R}^{2}))$ for every $q\in[1,2]$ , and, with $v=K_{BS}\ast\omega$ , for every $R>0$ and every $t\in[0,T)$ ,

$$ \int_{\{|x|\geq 2R\}}|\omega(t)|\differential x\leq\int_{\{|x|\geq R\}}|\omega^{\mathrm{in}}|\differential x+\frac{\|\nabla\varsigma\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}}{R}\,\|\omega v\|_{L^{1}((0,T)\times\mathbb{R}^{2})}, $$

where $\|\omega v\|_{L^{1}((0,T)\times\mathbb{R}^{2})}\leq C_{\mathrm{v}}TM^{2}$ with $M=\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\|\omega(t)\|_{(L^{1}\cap L^{2})(\mathbb{R}^{2})}$ .

#### Proof.

The number $M$ is finite by Lemma 3.2(a), and $\|\omega(t)v(t)\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\leq C_{\mathrm{v}}M^{2}$ for almost every $t$ by Lemma 2.2(a); this gives the bound on $\|\omega v\|_{L^{1}((0,T)\times\mathbb{R}^{2})}$ . By the remark at the start of Section 3.2, $v\in L^{\infty}(0,T;W^{1,2}(B_{R}))$ for every $R>0$ and $\divop v=0$ .

We first prove Equation (9). Let $t_{0}\in[0,T)$ and $\Upsilon\in\mathrm{Lip}_{0}$ . By Lemma 3.2(a) and (c), $\omega(t_{0})\in(L^{1}\cap L^{2})(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , and $\omega$ satisfies Equation (6) on $[t_{0},T)$ with field $v$ and datum $\omega(t_{0})$ , as well as on $[0,T)$ with datum $\omega^{\mathrm{in}}$ . Lemma 3.4(ii), applied on $[t_{0},T)$ and on $[0,T)$ and compared at a time $t\in(t_{0},T)$ that is exceptional for neither, gives $\int\Upsilon(\omega(t_{0}))=\int\Upsilon(\omega(t))=\int\Upsilon(\omega^{\mathrm{in}})$ . For $s,\delta>0$ the functions $z\mapsto\min\{1,(\pm z-s)_{+}/\delta\}$ lie in $\mathrm{Lip}_{0}$ and increase to $\mathbf{1}_{\{\pm z>s\}}$ as $\delta\downarrow 0$ , so monotone convergence gives the equimeasurability. Integration of the distribution function, $\int|g|^{q}=\int_{0}^{\infty}qs^{q-1}\big(|\{g>s\}|+|\{g<-s\}|\big)\differential s$ , $1\leq q<\infty$ , gives the norms.

Next, $\omega\in C([0,T);L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2}))$ : the norm $\|\omega(t)\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}$ is constant on $[0,T)$ , and $\omega$ is weakly continuous into $L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , so $\|\omega(t)-\omega(s)\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}^{2}=\|\omega(t)\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}^{2}+\|\omega(s)\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}^{2}-2\int\omega(t)\omega(s)\to 0$ as $t\to s$ . By Lemma 3.4(i) with $\Upsilon=|\cdot|$ , $|\omega|$ satisfies Equation (6) on $[0,T)$ with field $v$ and datum $|\omega^{\mathrm{in}}|$ . So Lemma 3.2 applies with $u=|\omega|$ , $w=v$ and $u_{0}=|\omega^{\mathrm{in}}|$ ; since $t\mapsto|\omega(t)|$ is continuous into $L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ on $[0,T)$ , it agrees there with the representative of that lemma, because two weakly continuous functions that agree for almost every $t$ agree for every $t$ . Part (b) of that lemma with $\psi=\varsigma_{R}$ , together with Equation (9) for $\Upsilon=|\cdot|$ , gives for every $t\in[0,T)$

$$ \int|\omega(t)|(1-\varsigma_{R})\differential x=\int|\omega^{\mathrm{in}}|(1-\varsigma_{R})\differential x-\int_{0}^{t}\!\!\int|\omega|\,v\cdot\nabla\varsigma_{R}\differential x\differential s. $$

Since $\mathbf{1}_{\{|x|\geq 2R\}}\leq 1-\varsigma_{R}\leq\mathbf{1}_{\{|x|\geq R\}}$ and $|\nabla\varsigma_{R}|\leq\|\nabla\varsigma\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}/R$ , this gives Equation (10). Its right side does not depend on $t$ and tends to $0$ as $R\to\infty$ . We split the $L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ norm into the parts on $B_{2R}$ and outside it: for $s,t\in[0,T)$ , by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality on $B_{2R}$ and Equation (10) for $\omega(t)$ and $\omega(s)$ ,

$$ \|\omega(t)-\omega(s)\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\leq|B_{2R}|^{1/2}\|\omega(t)-\omega(s)\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}+2\sup_{\tau\in[0,T)}\int_{\{|x|\geq 2R\}}|\omega(\tau)|\differential x. $$

Given $\eta>0$ , choose $R$ so that the last term is less than $\eta/2$ ; then the $L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ continuity makes the first term less than $\eta/2$ for $t$ close to $s$ . Hence $\omega\in C([0,T);L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2}))$ . Interpolation between $L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ and $L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ gives $\omega\in C([0,T);L^{q}(\mathbb{R}^{2}))$ for $q\in(1,2)$ . ∎

### 3.4 Radial Data and the Criterion

Recall from Section 2 that, for $g\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , $\Gamma_{g}(r)=\int_{B_{r}}g$ is the integral of $g$ over the disk $B_{r}$ ; for smooth $g$ it is the circulation of $K_{BS}\ast g$ around the circle $\{|x|=r\}$ .

#### Lemma 3.6.

Let $4/3<q<\infty$ , $T>0$ , and let $f\in(L^{1}\cap L^{q})(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ be radial. Then $K_{BS}\ast f(x)=\Gamma_{f}(|x|)\,x^{\perp}/(2\pi|x|^{2})$ for almost every $x$ , and $\omega(t)=f$ , $t\in[0,T]$ , is a renormalized weak solution in $X_{q}(T)$ with datum $f$ .

#### Proof.

We first prove the formula for radial $h=h_{0}(|\cdot|)\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ . We identify $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ with $\mathbb{C}$ , so that $z^{\perp}=iz$ and $K_{BS}(z)=i/(2\pi\bar{z})$ . By Lemma 2.1(e), for almost every $x\neq 0$ the integral defining $K_{BS}\ast h(x)$ converges absolutely, and in polar coordinates $y=se^{i\vartheta}$ ,

$$ K_{BS}\ast h(x)=\frac{i}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{\infty}h_{0}(s)\,s\int_{0}^{2\pi}\frac{\differential\vartheta}{\bar{x}-se^{-i\vartheta}}\differential s. $$

The inner integral equals $2\pi/\bar{x}$ for $s<|x|$ , by the uniformly convergent expansion $(\bar{x}-se^{-i\vartheta})^{-1}=\bar{x}^{-1}\sum_{l\geq 0}(s/\bar{x})^{l}e^{-il\vartheta}$ , and $0$ for $s>|x|$ , by the uniformly convergent expansion $(\bar{x}-se^{-i\vartheta})^{-1}=-s^{-1}e^{i\vartheta}\sum_{l\geq 0}(\bar{x}/s)^{l}e^{il\vartheta}$ , integrated term by term: $\int_{0}^{2\pi}e^{il\vartheta}\differential\vartheta=0$ for every integer $l\neq 0$ , so only the term $l=0$ of the first expansion survives, and no term of the second. Since $\Gamma_{h}(r)=2\pi\int_{0}^{r}h_{0}(s)s\differential s$ , we get

$$ K_{BS}\ast h(x)=\frac{i}{\bar{x}}\cdot\frac{\Gamma_{h}(|x|)}{2\pi}=\Gamma_{h}(|x|)\frac{x^{\perp}}{2\pi|x|^{2}}. $$

Now let $f=f_{0}(|\cdot|)$ , $v_{f}=K_{BS}\ast f$ , and $\Upsilon\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R})$ with $|\Upsilon^{\prime}|\leq L$ and $\Upsilon(0)=0$ . The constant function $\omega(t)=f$ lies in $X_{q}(T)$ and is weakly continuous, $\Upsilon(f)=\Upsilon(f_{0}(|\cdot|))$ is radial, and $|\Upsilon(f)v_{f}|\leq L|f||v_{f}|$ is integrable by Lemma 2.2(a). Let $\varphi\in\mathcal{D}_{T}$ . In polar coordinates $x=r(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$ we have $x^{\perp}\cdot\nabla=\partial_{\theta}$ , so the formula for $v_{f}$ gives $v_{f}\cdot\nabla\varphi(t)=\Gamma_{f}(r)(2\pi r^{2})^{-1}\partial_{\theta}\varphi(t)$ , and Fubini’s theorem gives, for every $t$ ,

$$ \int\Upsilon(f)\,v_{f}\cdot\nabla\varphi(t)\differential x=\int_{0}^{\infty}\Upsilon(f_{0}(r))\frac{\Gamma_{f}(r)}{2\pi r}\Big(\int_{0}^{2\pi}\partial_{\theta}\varphi(t)\differential\theta\Big)\differential r=0. $$

Since $\varphi(t)=0$ for $t$ near $T$ , we also have $\int_{0}^{T}\!\int\Upsilon(f)\partial_{t}\varphi\differential x\differential t=-\int\Upsilon(f)\varphi(0)\differential x$ . Hence Equation (5) holds, and Equation (4) is the case $\Upsilon(s)=s$ . ∎

#### Definition 3.7.

Let $f\in(L^{1}\cap L^{2})(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ . A $2$ -admissible sequence for $f$ on $[0,\infty)$ is a sequence of pairs $(f^{(n)},\omega^{(n)})_{n\geq 1}$ such that $f^{(n)}\in(L^{1}\cap L^{2})(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , $f^{(n)}\to f$ in $(L^{1}\cap L^{2})(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , and $\omega^{(n)}$ is a renormalized weak solution on $[0,\infty)$ with datum $f^{(n)}$ , in the sense of Definition 2.5 with $q=2$ .

#### Theorem 3.8.

Let $f\in(L^{1}\cap L^{2})(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ be radial, and let $(f^{(n)},\omega^{(n)})$ be a $2$ -admissible sequence for $f$ on $[0,\infty)$ . Assume that for some $T>0$

$$ c:=\limsup_{n\to\infty}\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}\|\omega^{(n)}(t)-f\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}>0. $$

Then there exists a subsequence $(n_{k})$ , together with a function $\omega_{\infty}\colon[0,\infty)\to(L^{1}\cap L^{2})(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , with the following properties.

- (i) $\omega_{\infty}$ is a renormalized weak solution on $[0,\infty)$ with datum $f$ , in the sense of Definition 2.5 with $q=2$ .

- (ii) For every $t\in[0,\infty)$ , $\omega_{\infty}(t)$ is equimeasurable with $f$ . Hence $\|\omega_{\infty}(t)\|_{L^{q}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}=\|f\|_{L^{q}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}$ for every $q\in[1,\infty)$ , and, whenever $f\in L^{q}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ with $q\in(4/3,\infty)$ , $\omega_{\infty}\in X_{q}(T^{\prime})$ for every $T^{\prime}>0$ .

- (iii) $\omega_{\infty}\in C([0,\infty);L^{q}(\mathbb{R}^{2}))$ whenever $f\in L^{q}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ with $q\in[1,\infty)$ .

- (iv) $\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}\|\omega^{(n_{k})}(t)-\omega_{\infty}(t)\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\to 0$ .

- (v) $\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}\|\omega_{\infty}(t)-f\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}=c$ . The set $\mathcal{O}=\{t\in[0,\infty):\omega_{\infty}(t)\neq f\}$ is open, $0\notin\mathcal{O}$ , and $\mathcal{O}\cap(0,T]\neq\emptyset$ . With $t_{0}=\inf\mathcal{O}\in[0,T)$ , $\omega_{\infty}$ and the stationary solution $f$ are distinct elements of $X_{q}(T^{\prime})$ for every $T^{\prime}>t_{0}$ , whenever $f\in L^{q}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ with $q\in(4/3,\infty)$ .

- (vi) If $\omega^{(n)}(t)$ is $3$ -fold rotationally symmetric for all $n$ and $t$ , then so is $\omega_{\infty}(t)$ for every $t$ .

#### Proof.

Write $\omega_{n}=\omega^{(n)}$ and $f_{n}=f^{(n)}$ . We first construct the limit. Pass to a subsequence along which $\sup_{t\leq T}\|\omega_{n}(t)-f\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\to c$ , and put $T_{j}=T+j$ for $j\geq 1$ . For $t\geq 0$ choose $j$ with $T_{j}>t$ ; by Definition 3.7, $\omega_{n}$ is a renormalized weak solution in $X_{2}(T_{j})$ , so Lemma 3.5 gives $\|\omega_{n}(t)\|_{L^{r}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}=\|f_{n}\|_{L^{r}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}$ for $r\in\{1,2\}$ . Hence $M:=\sup_{n}\sup_{t\geq 0}\|\omega_{n}(t)\|_{(L^{1}\cap L^{2})(\mathbb{R}^{2})}=\sup_{n}\|f_{n}\|_{(L^{1}\cap L^{2})(\mathbb{R}^{2})}<\infty$ , since $f_{n}$ converges in $(L^{1}\cap L^{2})(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ ; in particular $c\leq M+\|f\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}<\infty$ .

Write $v_{n}=K_{BS}\ast\omega_{n}$ , and let $\mathcal{F}$ be as in the proof of Lemma 3.2. Since $\|v_{n}(t)\|_{L^{2}(B_{R})}\leq C(2,R)M$ by Lemma 2.2(a), Lemma 3.2(b) on $[0,T_{j}]$ shows that the functions $t\mapsto\int\omega_{n}(t)\psi$ , $\psi\in\mathcal{F}$ , are bounded by $M\|\psi\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}$ and Lipschitz on every $[0,T_{j}]$ with a constant that depends neither on $n$ nor on $j$ . By the Arzelà-Ascoli theorem and a diagonal argument over $\psi\in\mathcal{F}$ and $j$ , a subsequence $(n_{k})$ converges uniformly on every $[0,T_{j}]$ for every $\psi\in\mathcal{F}$ ; below, $n$ runs through $(n_{k})$ . Since $|\int(\omega_{n}(t)-\omega_{m}(t))\psi|\leq 2M\|\psi-\psi^{\prime}\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}+|\int(\omega_{n}(t)-\omega_{m}(t))\psi^{\prime}|$ for $\psi\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ and $\psi^{\prime}\in\mathcal{F}$ , and $\mathcal{F}$ is dense in $L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , $\int\omega_{n}(t)\psi$ is uniformly Cauchy on every $[0,T_{j}]$ for every $\psi\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ . For each $t$ the limit is a linear functional of norm at most $M$ , hence $\psi\mapsto\int\omega_{\infty}(t)\psi$ for a unique $\omega_{\infty}(t)\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ . This gives the uniform weak convergence

$$ \sup_{t\leq T_{j}}\Big|\int(\omega_{n}(t)-\omega_{\infty}(t))\psi\Big|\to 0\qquad\text{for every }\psi\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})\text{ and every }j, $$

and $\omega_{\infty}$ is weakly continuous into $L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , as a locally uniform limit of the continuous functions $t\mapsto\int\omega_{n}(t)\psi$ .

Thus $\omega_{n}(t)\rightharpoonup\omega_{\infty}(t)$ weakly in $L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ for every $t$ . Fix $t\geq 0$ . Weak lower semicontinuity of the $L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ norm gives $\|\omega_{\infty}(t)\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\leq\liminf_{n}\|\omega_{n}(t)\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}$ . For the $L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ norm, put $\lambda=\liminf_{n}\|\omega_{n}(t)\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}$ and let $\varepsilon>0$ . There is a further subsequence $(\omega_{n_{i}}(t))_{i\geq 1}$ with $\|\omega_{n_{i}}(t)\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\leq\lambda+\varepsilon$ for every $i$ ; its terms are real, and it still converges weakly in $L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ to $\omega_{\infty}(t)$ . The first conclusion of Lemma 2.2(b), with $p=2$ , applied to this subsequence with $\lambda+\varepsilon$ in the role of the bound $M$ there, gives $\|\omega_{\infty}(t)\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\leq\lambda+\varepsilon$ . As $\varepsilon>0$ is arbitrary, $\|\omega_{\infty}(t)\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\leq\liminf_{n}\|\omega_{n}(t)\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}$ . Hence $\|\omega_{\infty}(t)\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}+\|\omega_{\infty}(t)\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\leq\liminf_{n}\big(\|\omega_{n}(t)\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}+\|\omega_{n}(t)\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\big)\leq M$ , so $\sup_{t\geq 0}\|\omega_{\infty}(t)\|_{(L^{1}\cap L^{2})(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\leq M$ . For $\phi\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , $t\mapsto\int\omega_{\infty}(t)\phi$ is the pointwise limit of the continuous functions $t\mapsto\int\omega_{\infty}(t)\phi\mathbf{1}_{B_{\ell}}$ as $\ell\to\infty$ . So $\omega_{\infty}$ is weakly measurable into $L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ and into $L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , hence strongly measurable into both by Pettis’s theorem (Section 2), as $L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ and $L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ are separable; with the bound by $M$ and the convention on intersections in Section 2, $\omega_{\infty}\in X_{2}(T_{j})$ for every $j$ .

Lemma 2.2(b) with $p=2$ and the uniform weak convergence give $v_{n}(t)\to v(t):=K_{BS}\ast\omega_{\infty}(t)$ in $L^{2}(B_{R})$ for every $t$ , and $\|v_{n}(t)-v(t)\|_{L^{2}(B_{R})}\leq 2C(2,R)M$ ; so dominated convergence in $t$ gives $\int_{0}^{T_{j}}\|v_{n}-v\|_{L^{2}(B_{R})}\differential t\to 0$ for every $j$ and $R>0$ . Now let $\varphi\in\mathcal{D}_{T_{j}}$ with $\supp\varphi\subset\mathbb{R}\times B_{R}$ . By the uniform weak convergence and dominated convergence in $t$ , with the bound $2M\|\partial_{t}\varphi(t)\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}$ , $\int_{0}^{T_{j}}\!\int\omega_{n}\partial_{t}\varphi\to\int_{0}^{T_{j}}\!\int\omega_{\infty}\partial_{t}\varphi$ ; and $\int f_{n}\varphi(0)\to\int f\varphi(0)$ , because $f_{n}\to f$ in $L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ . In

$$ \int_{0}^{T_{j}}\!\!\int(\omega_{n}v_{n}-\omega_{\infty}v)\cdot\nabla\varphi=\int_{0}^{T_{j}}\!\!\int\omega_{n}(v_{n}-v)\cdot\nabla\varphi+\int_{0}^{T_{j}}\!\!\int(\omega_{n}-\omega_{\infty})\,v\cdot\nabla\varphi, $$

the first term on the right is at most $M\|\nabla\varphi\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{2})}\int_{0}^{T_{j}}\|v_{n}-v\|_{L^{2}(B_{R})}\differential t\to 0$ . In the second term on the right, the inner integral tends to $0$ for each $t$ by the uniform weak convergence, because $v(t)\cdot\nabla\varphi(t)\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , and is bounded by $2C(2,R)M^{2}\|\nabla\varphi\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{2})}$ ; so dominated convergence applies. Thus Equation (4) for $\omega_{n}$ on $[0,T_{j})$ passes to the limit, and $\omega_{\infty}$ is a weak solution in $X_{2}(T_{j})$ with datum $f$ for every $j$ ; being weakly continuous, it is its own representative in the sense of Lemma 3.2. For $T^{\prime}>0$ choose $T_{j}>T^{\prime}$ ; since $\mathcal{D}_{T^{\prime}}\subset\mathcal{D}_{T_{j}}$ , the restriction of $\omega_{\infty}$ to $[0,T^{\prime}]$ is a weak solution in $X_{2}(T^{\prime})$ with datum $f$ , and it is renormalized: by the remark at the start of Section 3.2, Lemma 3.4(i) with $t_{0}=0$ , $u=\omega_{\infty}$ and $w=K_{BS}\ast\omega_{\infty}$ gives Equation (6) on $[0,T^{\prime})$ for $\Upsilon(\omega_{\infty})$ with datum $\Upsilon(f)$ , for every $\Upsilon\in\mathrm{Lip}_{0}$ , in particular for every $\Upsilon\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R})$ with $\Upsilon^{\prime}$ bounded and $\Upsilon(0)=0$ ; this is Equation (5). This proves (i).

We next prove (ii) and (iii). By Lemma 3.5, applied to $\omega_{\infty}$ on each $[0,T_{j})$ , $\omega_{\infty}(t)$ and $f$ are equimeasurable for every $t\geq 0$ , and integration of the distribution function gives $\|\omega_{\infty}(t)\|_{L^{q}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}=\|f\|_{L^{q}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}$ for $q\in[1,\infty)$ . For (iii), the case $q\in[1,2]$ is part of Lemma 3.5. Let $s_{i}\to t$ in $[0,\infty)$ , and put $g_{i}=\omega_{\infty}(s_{i})$ and $g=\omega_{\infty}(t)$ . Then $g_{i}\rightharpoonup g$ weakly in $L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ by weak continuity of $\omega_{\infty}$ , and $\|g_{i}\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}=\|g\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}$ , so $\|g_{i}-g\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}^{2}=2\|g\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}^{2}-2\int g_{i}g\to 0$ . Let $q\in(2,\infty)$ with $f\in L^{q}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , and let $K>0$ . Where $|g_{i}|\leq K$ and $|g|\leq K$ we have $|g_{i}-g|^{q}\leq(2K)^{q-2}|g_{i}-g|^{2}$ . On the remaining set, where $|g_{i}|>K$ or $|g|>K$ , we have $|g_{i}-g|^{q}\leq 2^{q}\max\{|g_{i}|,|g|\}^{q}\leq 2^{q}\big(|g_{i}|^{q}\mathbf{1}_{\{|g_{i}|>K\}}+|g|^{q}\mathbf{1}_{\{|g|>K\}}\big)$ . Integrating these two bounds gives

$$ \|g_{i}-g\|_{L^{q}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}^{q}\leq(2K)^{q-2}\|g_{i}-g\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}^{2}+2^{q}\Big(\int_{\{|g_{i}|>K\}}|g_{i}|^{q}\differential x+\int_{\{|g|>K\}}|g|^{q}\differential x\Big). $$

The last two integrals depend only on distribution functions. For $h\in L^{q}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , write $|h|^{q}=K^{q}+\int_{K}^{|h|}qs^{q-1}\differential s$ on $\{|h|>K\}$ and integrate in $x$ ; Tonelli’s theorem gives

$$ \int_{\{|h|>K\}}|h|^{q}\differential x=K^{q}\,|\{|h|>K\}|+\int_{K}^{\infty}qs^{q-1}\,|\{|h|>s\}|\differential s. $$

Since $g_{i}$ and $g$ are equimeasurable with $f$ by (ii), the measure $|\{|h|>s\}|=|\{h>s\}|+|\{h<-s\}|$ is the same for $h=g_{i}$ , $g$ and $f$ , for every $s>0$ . Hence both integrals equal $\int_{\{|f|>K\}}|f|^{q}\differential x$ , and

$$ \|g_{i}-g\|_{L^{q}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}^{q}\leq(2K)^{q-2}\|g_{i}-g\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}^{2}+2^{q+1}\int_{\{|f|>K\}}|f|^{q}\differential x, $$

and letting $i\to\infty$ and then $K\to\infty$ gives $g_{i}\to g$ in $L^{q}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ . This proves (iii). Now let $q\in(4/3,\infty)$ with $f\in L^{q}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ and $T^{\prime}>0$ . By (iii) and the norm identities, $\omega_{\infty}$ is continuous from $[0,T^{\prime}]$ into $(L^{1}\cap L^{q})(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , so $\omega_{\infty}\in X_{q}(T^{\prime})$ . This proves (ii).

We now prove (iv). Fix $j$ with $T<T_{j}$ . We claim: if $(n_{i})$ is a subsequence of $(n_{k})$ and $t_{i}\in[0,T]$ with $t_{i}\to t$ , then $\omega_{n_{i}}(t_{i})\to\omega_{\infty}(t)$ in $L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ . Granting the claim, if (iv) failed, there would be $\epsilon>0$ , a subsequence $(n_{i})$ and $t_{i}\in[0,T]$ with $\|\omega_{n_{i}}(t_{i})-\omega_{\infty}(t_{i})\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\geq\epsilon$ ; along a further subsequence $t_{i}\to t\in[0,T]$ , and the claim and (iii) give $\|\omega_{n_{i}}(t_{i})-\omega_{\infty}(t_{i})\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\to 0$ , a contradiction.

To prove the claim, write $n$ for $n_{i}$ . For $\psi\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ ,

$$ \Big|\int(\omega_{n}(t_{i})-\omega_{\infty}(t))\psi\Big|\leq\sup_{s\leq T_{j}}\Big|\int(\omega_{n}(s)-\omega_{\infty}(s))\psi\Big|+\Big|\int(\omega_{\infty}(t_{i})-\omega_{\infty}(t))\psi\Big|\to 0, $$

by the uniform weak convergence on $[0,T_{j}]$ and weak continuity of $\omega_{\infty}$ . By the norm identities for $\omega_{n}$ above and part (ii), $\|\omega_{n}(t_{i})\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}=\|f_{n}\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\to\|f\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}=\|\omega_{\infty}(t)\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}$ ; expanding $\|\omega_{n}(t_{i})-\omega_{\infty}(t)\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}^{2}$ shows that $\omega_{n}(t_{i})\to\omega_{\infty}(t)$ in $L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , hence in $L^{1}(B_{2R})$ for every $R>0$ . Letting $n\to\infty$ and then $R\to\infty$ proves the claim.

We now prove (v). By (iv),

$$ \Big|\sup_{t\leq T}\|\omega_{n}(t)-f\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}-\sup_{t\leq T}\|\omega_{\infty}(t)-f\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\Big|\leq\sup_{t\leq T}\|\omega_{n}(t)-\omega_{\infty}(t)\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\to 0, $$

so the second supremum equals $c>0$ . By (iii) with $q=1$ , $t\mapsto\|\omega_{\infty}(t)-f\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}$ is continuous on $[0,\infty)$ , so $\mathcal{O}$ is relatively open in $[0,\infty)$ , and it meets $[0,T]$ . so $\omega_{\infty}(t)\circ\mathsf{O}=\omega_{\infty}(t)$ almost everywhere. ∎

#### Corollary 3.9.

Let $f\in(L^{1}\cap L^{q})(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ for every $q\in[1,\infty)$ be radial. Let $m\geq 1$ be an integer, $\chi\in C_{c}^{\infty}((0,\infty))$ real, and $\Psi(x)=\chi(|x|)\,(\bar{x})^{m}$ (with $x$ written as a complex number). Let $(f^{(n)},\omega^{(n)})$ be a $2$ -admissible sequence for $f$ on $[0,\infty)$ such that $\omega^{(n)}(t)$ is $3$ -fold rotationally symmetric for all $n$ and $t$ . Assume that there are $c_{0}>0$ , $\bar{T}\in(0,\infty)$ and times $T^{(n)}\in[0,\bar{T}]$ with

$$ \Big|\int\omega^{(n)}(T^{(n)})\,\Psi\Big|\geq c_{0}\qquad\text{for all large }n. $$

Then there is a renormalized weak solution $\omega_{\infty}$ on $[0,\infty)$ with datum $f$ , in the sense of Definition 2.5 with $q=2$ , such that $\omega_{\infty}(t)$ is equimeasurable with $f$ and $3$ -fold rotationally symmetric for every $t\geq 0$ , $\omega_{\infty}\in C([0,\infty);L^{q}(\mathbb{R}^{2}))$ for every $q\in[1,\infty)$ , and, for some $t_{0}\in[0,\bar{T})$ , $\omega_{\infty}$ and $f$ are distinct elements of $X_{q}(T^{\prime})$ for every $T^{\prime}>t_{0}$ and every $q\in(4/3,\infty)$ .

#### Proof.

Write $f=f_{0}(|\cdot|)$ . Since $\chi$ has compact support in $(0,\infty)$ , the function $\Psi$ lies in $C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2};\mathbb{C})$ , and in polar coordinates $\int f\Psi=\int_{0}^{\infty}f_{0}(r)\chi(r)r^{m+1}\big(\int_{0}^{2\pi}e^{-im\theta}\differential\theta\big)\differential r=0$ , because $m\neq 0$ . $$ c_{0}\leq\Big|\int(\omega^{(n)}(T^{(n)})-f)\Psi\Big|\leq\|\Psi\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\sup_{t\leq\bar{T}}\|\omega^{(n)}(t)-f\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}. $$

Thus $\|\Psi\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}>0$ , and Equation (11) holds with $T=\bar{T}$ , with $c\geq c_{0}/\|\Psi\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}$ . #### Remark 3.10.

Corollary 3.9 is a conditional non-uniqueness theorem. Let $f$ be radial with $f\in(L^{1}\cap L^{q})(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ for every $q\in[1,\infty)$ .
